blocks.html: Picture Egypt from space at night and you see its whole history in one image: a thin bright line running north through dark desert, then a bright fan where the river spreads out before the sea. Almost everyone in ancient Egypt lived inside that line and that fan. This course begins with the land, because the land explains so much of what came after.

Ancient Egypt was the Nile valley, a ribbon of black farmland rarely more than about 20 km wide, and the Delta, the fan of land where the river splits into branches before reaching the Mediterranean. Deserts lay on both sides.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The Nile valley and the Delta. Drag to pan, zoom in on the valley, and tap a site for its note. The dark strip along the river is where people lived.

blocks.html: Egyptians called their farmland Kemet, "the black land", after the dark mud the river left behind, and the desert Deshret, "the red land". The line between them was sharp: you could stand with one foot in a green field and the other on bare sand. Villages, towns and fields crowded the black land. The red land was for cemeteries, quarries and mines, and for the roads to the oases, the Red Sea and Nubia.

The Nile is the only large river that crosses the Sahara from south to north, and Egypt gets almost no rain. Without the river there would be no farming at all. So people settled where the water and the mud were, and the shape of the river became the shape of the country.

items: The valley (Upper Egypt): from the First Cataract at Aswan north to about Memphis, near modern Cairo. Thebes (Luxor), Abydos and Elephantine lie here.
The Delta (Lower Egypt): from Memphis to the sea, wide, flat and marshy, with branches of the river and later cities such as Tanis and Alexandria.
The Faiyum: a fertile basin west of the valley, fed by a branch of the Nile.
The deserts: the Western Desert with its oases (Siwa, Kharga), and the Eastern Desert between the Nile and the Red Sea, with gold mines and quarries.
The cataracts: rocky rapids south of Aswan that made the river hard to sail. The First Cataract was Egypt's usual southern border.

blocks.title: Reading the map
blocks.q: Thebes lies at about 25.7° N and Memphis at about 29.8° N. Which is upstream, and why does that matter for travel?
steps: The Nile flows from south to north, so the more southern city is upstream.
Thebes is farther south (a smaller latitude), so Thebes is upstream of Memphis.
Boats going north from Thebes to Memphis floated with the current; boats going south raised a sail, because the wind in Egypt usually blows from the north.
blocks.a: Thebes is upstream. The river carried boats north, and the north wind pushed them back south.

blocks.html: Picturing Egypt as a broad country full of people. On a modern map Egypt is a big square, but nearly all ancient Egyptians lived in the narrow valley and the Delta. The deserts held mines, quarries, oases and trade routes, not farms or cities. A quick check: if a place is far from the river and is not an oasis, it was not a farming town.

blocks.html: In the last lesson you saw that Egypt lived on the Nile. Every summer the river did something that shaped the whole year: it rose, spilled over its banks and covered the valley floor with water for weeks. Egyptians called this akhet, the inundation.

The flood came from summer monsoon rains on the Ethiopian highlands, far to the south, carried down the Blue Nile and the Atbara. It reached Egypt in summer, covered the fields, and left a layer of fresh silt. The height of the flood decided whether the harvest would be good.

Two rivers make the Nile. The White Nile, from the lakes of East Africa, flows steadily all year. The Blue Nile, from the Ethiopian highlands, swells hugely when the summer rains fall there and carries most of the mud. When that surge reached Egypt, the river rose by several meters. Egypt itself had almost no rain; the water and the soil both came from far away.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The Nile from Sudan to the sea. The flood water came from much farther south, beyond the edge of this map.

blocks.text: Too high, too low, just right

blocks.html: A good flood soaked the basins of farmland and drained away in time to plant. A low flood left fields dry and meant hunger. A very high flood swept away dikes and villages. So the Egyptians measured the river. Nilometers, stairs or wells with marked levels, recorded each year's height, and officials used the readings to estimate the harvest and set taxes. One famous nilometer is on Elephantine Island at Aswan.

head: Season
Egyptian name
What happened
rows: The fields were under water; farm work stopped, and many people could be called up for building work.
The land came out of the water; farmers plowed, sowed and tended wheat, barley and flax.
Grain was cut, threshed and stored; the river was at its lowest.
blocks.cap: Each season had four months of 30 days. Five extra days at the end made a year of 365 days.

blocks.title: Why a low flood mattered
blocks.q: A scribe records a flood well below normal. What does he expect next, and who needs to know?
steps: Less water means fewer fields are soaked, so less land can be sown.
Less land sown means a smaller harvest of grain.
The granaries and the tax officials need to know, because taxes were set from the expected harvest.
blocks.a: A smaller harvest, so lower taxes and careful use of stored grain.

blocks.html: Thinking the flood came from rain in Egypt. Egypt is one of the driest places on earth; the flood came from monsoon rains on the Ethiopian highlands, thousands of kilometers south. Check: the flood arrived in high summer, the driest time in Egypt itself.
Since the Aswan High Dam was finished in 1970, the flood no longer reaches Egypt; Lake Nasser holds the water back.

blocks.html: Egyptians did not usually call their country "Egypt" (that name came later, from Greek). They called it Kemet, the black land, or the Two Lands. The phrase shows how they thought about the country: one kingdom made of two halves, the long valley and the wide Delta, joined under one king.

Upper Egypt is the south, the valley upstream from Memphis to Aswan. Lower Egypt is the north, the Delta. The country was divided into provinces called nomes, each with its capital, its gods and, at times, a powerful governor.

"Upper" and "lower" follow the river, not the map. The Nile flows from south to north, so the south is upriver, "upper", and the north is downriver, "lower". Modern maps put north at the top, which makes this feel backward.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Upper Egypt runs from the First Cataract north to near Memphis; Lower Egypt is the Delta. Nekhen (Hierakonpolis) and Buto were early centers of the south and the north.

blocks.cap: nsw-bjt, "King of Upper and Lower Egypt": the sedge for the south and the bee for the north.

blocks.html: Egypt was divided into about 42 nomes: about 22 in Upper Egypt and about 20 in Lower Egypt (the number changed over time). Each nome had a capital town, a local god and a standard, a sign on a pole that served as its emblem. Under a strong king, the nomes were run by officials sent out by the court. When the center was weak, nome governors (nomarchs) acted like local princes. You will see this pattern again in the 6th Dynasty and the First Intermediate Period.

blocks.title: Which way is up?
blocks.q: A traveler sails from Memphis to Thebes. Is she going into Upper Egypt or Lower Egypt?
steps: Thebes is south of Memphis.
South is upstream on the Nile, and upstream is "Upper".
So she is sailing into Upper Egypt, against the current.
blocks.a: Upper Egypt.

blocks.html: Putting Upper Egypt in the north because it is at the top of the map. Upper and Lower follow the river: Upper Egypt is the south. A check: the Delta, at the top of a modern map, is Lower Egypt, because it is where the river ends.

blocks.html: How do we know any of this? No ancient Egyptian wrote a history of Egypt in the way a modern historian does. Instead, historians piece the past together from many kinds of evidence, each useful and each with its own point of view.

Historians use monuments and inscriptions, papyri and ostraca (notes on pottery or stone flakes), archaeology (houses, tombs, objects, bones, seeds), foreign records (letters, treaties and annals of other kingdoms), and later Greek and Roman writers. Every source has a purpose and a bias.

blocks.html: A source is made by someone, for someone. A king's temple wall was made to show the gods and the people that he kept order and defeated chaos, so a battle that went badly would not appear as a defeat. Asking "who made this, and why?" is the first step in using any source.

Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs on stone and in the quicker hieratic script on papyrus and ostraca; later came Demotic, and in Christian times Coptic. Papyrus survives mostly in the dry desert edge, so some places and periods are far better documented than others. The wet Delta, where great cities stood, has lost almost all its papyri.

blocks.cap: The stages of the Egyptian language and its scripts. Each kind of writing tends to preserve a different kind of source.

blocks.title: Comparing two sources
blocks.q: An Egyptian temple says the king won a great victory at a battle. A letter from the enemy's archive says the enemy kept control of the disputed town. What should a historian conclude?
steps: Both sources had reasons to praise their own side.
The outcome on the ground (who held the town afterward) is harder to spin than a description of the fighting.
So the historian treats the temple account as the king's version and weighs it against the letter and the later situation.
blocks.a: The result was probably not the clear victory the temple claims; the evidence must be weighed together.

blocks.html: You will meet exactly this problem at the battle of Kadesh.

Taking royal inscriptions at face value. Kings recorded victories, gifts from the gods and perfect order, not defeats or failures. Check every claim against a second kind of evidence: archaeology, a foreign record, or what happened afterward.

blocks.html: Egyptian history runs for about three thousand years of kings, from about 3000 BC to the Roman conquest in 30 BC, and Egypt's story continues after that. To find our way through so much time, modern historians divide it into big blocks. Learning these blocks first makes everything else easier to place.

Kingdoms (Old, Middle, New) were times when one strong government ruled all of Egypt. Intermediate Periods (First, Second, Third) were times when power was divided among rival rulers. These are modern labels, not names the Egyptians used.

blocks.name: eg-timeline

blocks.html: The labels began in the 1800s, when scholars noticed that the monuments clustered into three great ages of building, separated by times with few big monuments and many local rulers. The kingdoms became "Old", "Middle" and "New", and the gaps "intermediate". The Egyptians themselves counted time by kings, not by periods.

blocks.title: Placing a date
blocks.q: In which period does c. 1800 BC fall?
steps: The Middle Kingdom runs from c. 2055 to c. 1650 BC.
BC years count down toward year 1, so 1800 lies between 2055 and 1650.
1800 is far from both ends, so the uncertainty in the dates does not matter here.
blocks.a: The Middle Kingdom.

blocks.html: Thinking the Egyptians used these names. "Old Kingdom" and "Intermediate Period" are modern tools. Also, an "intermediate" period was not empty: people farmed, built and wrote; power was simply shared out. A check: if a label sounds like a judgment, ask who made it and when.
In BC dates bigger numbers are earlier: c. 2055 BC comes before c. 1650 BC.

blocks.html: The periods are a modern framework. But the Egyptians themselves kept lists of their kings, and these lists are the backbone of the chronology. They also show us something important: which kings later Egyptians chose to remember.

Ancient king lists give rulers in order, sometimes with the length of each reign. The main ones are the Palermo Stone (Old Kingdom annals), the Turin King List (a papyrus with reign lengths), and the lists carved at Abydos, Karnak and Saqqara. None is complete, and some leave rulers out on purpose.

blocks.html: The carved lists were not history books. At Abydos, Seti I and his son stand offering to the names of the earlier kings, the ancestors whose spirits received offerings in the temple. Only kings counted as rightful belonged there. Hatshepsut, a woman who ruled as king, and the Amarna kings, linked to Akhenaten's break with the old gods, were left out.

blocks.title: Spot the gap
blocks.q: The Abydos list names Amenhotep III and then Horemheb. Using the timeline, which kings who really ruled are missing between them?
steps: After Amenhotep III came Akhenaten, then a short reign or two (including Smenkhkare), then Tutankhamun and Ay.
Horemheb came after Ay.
So the list skips the whole Amarna group.
blocks.a: Akhenaten, Smenkhkare, Tutankhamun and Ay.

blocks.html: The Turin King List is different: an administrative papyrus that tried to list every ruler with his years, months and days, and even includes kings the temple lists ignore. Sadly it was broken into hundreds of pieces before it reached Turin, and many entries are lost.

Treating a king list as complete. Lists leave out rejected rulers, skip whole periods, and sometimes list rival kings who ruled at the same time as if they came one after another. A check: compare at least two lists and the monuments of the kings themselves.

blocks.html: Why do we say "the 18th Dynasty" or "the 4th Dynasty"? The numbers come from one man, an Egyptian priest named Manetho, who lived in the early 3rd century BC under the first Ptolemies. He wrote a history of Egypt in Greek, the Aegyptiaca, using temple records and king lists like the ones in the last lesson.

Manetho grouped the kings into 30 dynasties (a 31st was added later), from Menes to the last native kings. Historians still use his numbers. His book is lost; it survives only in quotations and summaries by later writers, such as Josephus, Africanus and Eusebius, which do not always agree.

A dynasty for Manetho was a group of kings he could treat together, often named for the city they came from ("the 12th Dynasty, of Thebes"; "the 26th, of Sais"). Usually that meant one family, but not always. Sometimes the line changed with the capital, and in divided times two or three of his dynasties ruled at the same time in different places.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The Third Intermediate Period: the dynasty bars below the periods show the 22nd, 23rd, 24th and 25th Dynasties overlapping in time.

items: Manetho wrote in Greek for the new Greek-speaking rulers of Egypt.
The Jewish historian Josephus (1st century AD) quoted parts of it, including the story of the Hyksos.
Christian chronologists, Julius Africanus and Eusebius, made lists of Manetho's dynasties and reign lengths; later writers copied those.
Copies of copies drifted: the same king can have different reign lengths in different versions.

blocks.title: Overlapping dynasties
blocks.q: A list gives the 22nd Dynasty c. 945–715 BC and the 23rd c. 818–715 BC. Did the 23rd Dynasty follow the 22nd?
steps: If the 23rd followed the 22nd, it would begin after c. 715 BC.
Instead it begins c. 818 BC, while the 22nd was still ruling.
So the two dynasties ruled at the same time, in different parts of Egypt.
blocks.a: No: they overlapped.

blocks.html: Thinking a dynasty is always one family. Manetho's divisions sometimes follow a change of capital rather than of bloodline, and dynasties in intermediate periods often overlap. Adding up all his dynasties end to end makes Egyptian history far too long, a mistake some early scholars made.
Manetho's numbering is a convenience. It is so useful that every Egyptologist uses it, even while knowing its flaws.

blocks.html: Today we count years in one long line: 1999, 2000, 2001. Egyptians did not. They dated documents by the king: "Year 5, second month of the harvest season, day 10, under the Majesty of King So-and-so." When a new king came to the throne, the count started again at Year 1.

Egyptian dates are regnal years: years of a king's reign. To turn them into years BC, historians must know the order of the kings and the length of each reign, and add them up king by king. Co-regencies (two kings ruling together) and gaps make this hard.

A regnal date tells you how far into one reign an event fell, but nothing about how long ago that reign was. To place it on our calendar, you need a chain: the lengths of all the reigns between it and some king whose date is known from another source. Each link in the chain has its own uncertainty, so errors add up the farther back you go.

blocks.title: An imaginary dynasty
blocks.q: Imagine three kings who ruled one after another. King A ruled 20 years, King B 12 years, King C 30 years. If King A's Year 1 was 1500 BC, in what year BC was King C's Year 1?
steps: King A's 20 years run from 1500 to 1481 BC (Year 1 is 1500, so Year 20 is 1500 − 19 = 1481).
King B's Year 1 is the next year, 1480 BC; his 12 years run to 1469 BC.
King C's Year 1 is the next year, 1468 BC. Shortcut: 1500 − (20 + 12) = 1468.
blocks.a: 1468 BC (in this imaginary example).

blocks.html: Real cases are messier. Reigns were counted in whole years, so the last part-year of one king and the first of the next can overlap. Some kings named their sons as co-rulers, so for a few years two reigns ran at once; how long some co-regencies lasted is still debated. And many reign lengths are missing from the king lists.

blocks.html: Expecting a continuous era like BC and AD. Each reign restarted the count. And because of co-regencies, simply adding all reign lengths can count some years twice. A check: does any king's reign overlap with the one before?

blocks.html: Adding up regnal years gives a chain of reigns, but the chain needs to be pinned to our calendar somewhere. A few Egyptian texts record events in the sky, and the sky runs like a clock. If an ancient observation can be matched to an exact astronomical date, a reign can be tied to a year BC.

Two kinds of observation help: the heliacal rising of Sirius (the first morning the star Sirius is seen again before dawn after weeks hidden by the sun), and dates of the moon's phases. They can tie reigns to absolute dates, but the results depend on where the observation was made and how the calendar worked, so scholars still debate them.

The Egyptian civil calendar had exactly 365 days, but the solar year is about 365¼ days. So the calendar slipped one day against the seasons every four years. The rising of Sirius, tied to the solar year, moved through the civil calendar, returning to the same calendar date only after about 1,460 years. A record saying "Sirius rose on month 4, day 16 in Year 7" tells you where in that long cycle you are.

blocks.title: How fast the calendar drifts
blocks.q: The civil calendar loses about one day every 4 years against the sun. How many years does it take to drift by a full 30-day month?
steps: One day of drift takes 4 years.
30 days of drift take 30 × 4 years.
blocks.a: About 120 years.

blocks.title: A whole cycle
blocks.q: How long until the drift adds up to a whole calendar year of 365 days?
steps: One day takes 4 years, so 365 days take 365 × 4 years.
blocks.a: About 1,460 years (the "Sothic cycle", from Sothis, the Greek name of Sirius).

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Reigns that astronomy helps to pin down: a Sirius record from Senusret III's reign, and moon dates for Thutmose III and Ramesses II.

blocks.html: A Roman writer, Censorinus, recorded that the Egyptian new year and the rising of Sirius fell together in AD 139. Counting back from that fixed point, scholars can date older records of Sirius: one from the reign of Senusret III (the Illahun papyri) and one from Amenhotep I (the Ebers papyrus).

blocks.text: Why the answer moves by decades

items: Sirius rises a few days later in the south than in the north. Was the observation made at Memphis, Thebes or Elephantine? Each choice shifts the date by decades.
Moon dates repeat every 11 or 25 years or so. For Ramesses II, the lunar data allow an accession in 1304, 1290 or 1279 BC; most scholars now prefer c. 1279 BC.
Scholars disagree about details of how the calendar was kept.

blocks.html: Taking astronomical dates as exact. An eclipse or a star rising is precise, but matching an ancient record to it depends on assumptions about place and calendar that change the result by decades. That is why this course writes "c." before every date earlier than 664 BC.

blocks.html: King lists and the stars are written evidence. Radiocarbon dating is a different kind: it reads a clock built into living things. It is especially useful for the times before writing, when there are no reigns to add up at all.

Radiocarbon dating measures how much carbon-14 is left in plant or animal remains. It gives a range of years, often several decades wide, not one exact year. Studies of short-lived plant remains from well-dated Egyptian contexts largely agree with the standard chronology.

Living things take in carbon from the air, including a tiny share of radioactive carbon-14. When they die, they stop taking it in, and the carbon-14 slowly decays: half of it is gone in about 5,700 years. Measuring what is left tells you how long ago the plant or animal died. Because the amount of carbon-14 in the air has varied, labs calibrate the result against tree rings, which turns it into a range of calendar years.

items: Short-lived plants (seeds, reeds, linen) are best: they died in the same year they grew.
Old wood can mislead: a beam might come from a tree that grew centuries before it was cut, or be reused.
The sample must come from a context tied to a king, such as grain from a sealed tomb of known date.

blocks.html: A large study published in 2010 (Bronk Ramsey and colleagues) dated more than 200 such samples from the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms. The results fit the historians' chronology in broad outline, with some dates a little earlier than many had used. For the Predynastic Period and the first dynasties, radiocarbon is our main tool: it places the beginning of the 1st Dynasty around 3100–3000 BC.

blocks.title: Reading a range
blocks.q: A lab reports a date of 1450 ± 40 BC for seeds from a tomb. What range of years does that cover?
steps: ± 40 means 40 years either side of 1450.
Earliest: 1450 + 40 = 1490 BC (bigger BC numbers are earlier).
blocks.a: From about 1490 to 1410 BC, a range of 80 years.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The end of the Predynastic Period and the Early Dynastic Period. Here radiocarbon dates do most of the work.

blocks.html: Thinking radiocarbon gives one exact year. It gives a range, often several decades wide, and the range can be wider where the calibration curve is flat. For the New Kingdom, the king lists are usually more precise; radiocarbon is a check on them, not a replacement.

blocks.html: You have now seen the tools: king lists, regnal years, astronomy and radiocarbon. Put together, how good are the dates? The answer depends on the period.

Egyptian dates are fixed to the year from 664 BC on, when Psamtek I became king; links to Assyrian, Babylonian and Greek records tie the reigns to our calendar. Before that, dates are approximate: uncertain by a decade or two in the New Kingdom, a few decades in the Middle Kingdom, and a century or more in the Old Kingdom and earlier.

blocks.html: Every date before 664 BC hangs on a chain of reign lengths reaching back from a fixed point. Each missing or uncertain reign adds to the error, so the error grows the farther back you go. Astronomy and radiocarbon pin the chain in a few places, but with uncertainties of their own.

You will see different dates in different books. Khufu's reign begins c. 2589 BC in Shaw's Oxford History; other respected chronologies place it a few decades earlier or later. They are all best estimates from the same evidence, weighed a little differently. That is why historians write "c." and why this course uses one chronology, Shaw (2000), consistently.

blocks.title: Can we tell?
blocks.q: A tomb is dated "c. 2165 BC" in one book. Can we be sure whether it belongs to the Old Kingdom or the First Intermediate Period?
steps: The boundary is placed at c. 2160 BC.
c. 2165 BC is only 5 years before that boundary.
The uncertainty in this part of the chronology is many decades, so a 5-year difference cannot decide it.
blocks.a: No. A date that close to a boundary cannot settle the question; other evidence (style, titles, inscriptions) must.

blocks.title: Counting across BC and AD
blocks.q: How many years passed from 30 BC, when Egypt became Roman, to AD 641?
steps: There is no year 0: 1 BC is followed by AD 1.
From 30 BC to 1 BC is 29 years; from 1 BC to AD 1 is 1 year; from AD 1 to AD 641 is 640 years.
blocks.a: 670 years. Shortcut: add the two numbers and subtract 1.

blocks.html: Quoting early dates as exact years. "Khufu began to reign in 2589 BC" sounds precise, but it is a best estimate. Write c. 2589 BC, and remember another book may give a different number.

blocks.html: Long before the first king, people were farming along the Nile. The pharaohs did not appear out of nowhere: they grew out of more than a thousand years of village life, trade and slowly growing chiefdoms in the two halves of the country.

Farming villages appeared along the Nile by the 5th millennium BC. In Upper Egypt the Badarian culture (c. 4400–4000 BC) was followed by the Naqada culture (c. 4000–3000 BC), which grew richer, spread north over the whole country, and developed into small kingdoms led by powerful chiefs.

Farming made it possible to store a surplus of grain. A surplus could feed craftsmen, traders and leaders who did not farm, and it could be taxed, traded or fought over. Over centuries, the villages that controlled the best land and trade routes grew into centers of power, such as Naqada, Hierakonpolis and Abydos.

blocks.html: In the Delta and around the Faiyum, other farming cultures (at Merimde and in the Faiyum, and later at Maadi and Buto) had their own pottery and houses. During Naqada II and III, Naqada-style pottery, burials and goods replaced the northern styles. Whether this happened through trade, migration, conquest or all three is still discussed.

Most of what we know comes from cemeteries. In the 1890s Flinders Petrie dug thousands of Predynastic graves, at Naqada and nearby sites, and worked out how to put them in order by the changing styles of their pottery, a method called sequence dating. Today radiocarbon gives the dates in years, and excavations of settlements at Hierakonpolis and elsewhere show houses, breweries and workshops.

blocks.title: Reading the evidence
blocks.q: In late Naqada graves, a few tombs are very large and full of fine goods, while most are small and simple. What does that suggest?
steps: Grave goods reflect what a family could afford to bury, and how they wanted the dead to be seen.
A few very rich tombs among many plain ones mean wealth was concentrated in a few hands.
That is a sign of a ranked society with leaders, the kind of society from which kings emerged.
blocks.a: A ranked society, with a small, wealthy ruling group.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptian civilization appeared suddenly. It grew over many centuries of village farming, crafts and trade. The first kings stand at the end of a long story, not the beginning. Claims that a lost outside civilization built early Egypt are rejected by archaeologists, because the gradual local development can be traced, grave by grave.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 3, The Naqada Period

blocks.html: Among the rulers of late Naqada times was one buried at Abydos in a large tomb that archaeologists call U-j. When German archaeologists led by Günter Dreyer excavated it in the late 1980s, they found something remarkable: over a hundred tiny labels of bone and ivory, each carved with a few signs.

The labels from tomb U-j at Abydos, from about c. 3200 BC, carry some of the earliest known Egyptian writing. They were probably tied to goods in the tomb and record things like places of origin or quantities. Exactly how to read them is still debated.

Writing grows out of a need to keep track. A ruler receiving goods from many places needed to know where each jar or bale came from and how much there was. Labels with a few signs (a number, a place, an estate) are just what early record-keeping looks like. Writing in Egypt seems to have begun as a tool of administration, then spread to royal display.

Some U-j labels show animals, plants, mountains or buildings; others carry numbers. Several signs already look like later hieroglyphs, and some may already stand for sounds, not just pictures. That is the key step that turns pictures into writing: using a sign for its sound. Later Egyptian writing mixes sound signs with word signs in just this way.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: A later hieroglyph, ḏw "mountain". Early writing already used pictures like this as signs, some of them for their sound.

blocks.html: Writing also appeared in southern Mesopotamia, at Uruk, at about the same time, around the late 4th millennium BC. Did one invent it and the other borrow the idea? The two scripts look completely different and were used in different ways, and the Egyptian evidence is now at least as early as the Mesopotamian. Scholars still debate whether there was any influence; many now think writing developed independently in both places.

blocks.title: Why the date matters
blocks.q: For a long time the earliest Egyptian writing known was later than Mesopotamia's, and many scholars assumed Egypt borrowed the idea. What did the U-j finds change?
steps: Radiocarbon and the style of the finds date tomb U-j to about c. 3200 BC or a little earlier.
That is about as early as the earliest Mesopotamian writing.
So simple borrowing became much less likely, and independent invention became a serious possibility.
blocks.a: They made Egyptian writing about as old as Mesopotamian writing, reopening the question.

blocks.html: Assuming Egyptians borrowed writing from Mesopotamia. Writing appeared in both at about the same time, in different forms; whether one influenced the other is debated. Present it as an open question.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 3

blocks.html: By the end of the Naqada period, a few powerful kingdoms in Upper Egypt were growing at the expense of their neighbors. Around c. 3000 BC, the whole country, from the First Cataract to the sea, came under one ruler. Egyptians later remembered this as the joining of the Two Lands.

Around c. 3000 BC the Nile valley and the Delta came under one king. The Narmer Palette, found at Hierakonpolis, shows King Narmer wearing the White Crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the Red Crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Unification was probably a long process, not a single battle.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Hierakonpolis (Nekhen), where the palette was found, and Memphis, the capital founded near the meeting point of the valley and the Delta.

blocks.html: The palette is a shield-shaped slab of dark stone about 64 cm tall, of the kind used for grinding eye paint but far too large and fine for daily use. It was found in 1897–98 in a temple deposit at Hierakonpolis and is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. On one side Narmer, in the tall White Crown, raises a mace over a kneeling enemy. On the other he wears the Red Crown and walks in procession toward rows of beheaded foes. His name is written at the top in a serekh, a palace façade: a catfish (nꜥr) and a chisel (mr).

A palette dedicated in a temple was a gift to the gods. Its scenes show what a king should do: defeat enemies, bring order, rule both lands. They are a statement of kingship, not a news report. That is why historians use the palette as evidence that one king claimed both crowns, not as a record of one particular day.

Later Egyptians and Manetho named the first king Menes. No contemporary monument names Menes clearly. Many scholars think Menes was Narmer; others think he was Narmer's successor, Aha. Before Narmer came a series of rulers archaeologists call "Dynasty 0", buried at Abydos, who already controlled much of the country.

blocks.title: Evidence for a process
blocks.q: Royal names from "Dynasty 0" have been found on jars in the Delta, and Naqada culture had spread north before Narmer. What does that suggest about unification?
steps: Southern rulers' goods and styles were already in the north before Narmer.
So southern influence, trade and perhaps control grew over several generations.
Narmer may have completed, or simply proclaimed, a union that was long under way.
blocks.a: Unification was gradual; Narmer stands near its end.

blocks.html: Treating the palette as a news photo of one battle. It is a ceremonial object showing ideal kingship. Unification was probably a long process of trade, alliance and war across Naqada II and III. A check: ask what the maker wanted the gods and viewers to believe.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 4, The Emergence of the Egyptian State

blocks.html: The joining of the Two Lands gave Egypt one king. The next three centuries, Dynasties 1 and 2 (c. 3000–2686 BC), built the machinery that kept the country together. Pyramids were still in the future; this was the age of mud brick, of seals and labels, and of the first royal titles.

Kings of the 1st and 2nd Dynasties (c. 3000–2686 BC) ruled from Memphis, near the meeting point of the valley and the Delta, and were buried at Abydos. They built the tools of the state: writing for records, taxes counted by royal officials, and the king's titles.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The Early Dynastic Period, before the Old Kingdom.

blocks.html: Memphis sits where the narrow valley opens into the Delta. From there a king could watch the river traffic between south and north and reach both halves quickly. Abydos, in the south, was the old burial ground of the rulers from whom the kings came, so they kept burying there.

items: Writing and seals: jar labels and seal impressions record goods, estates and officials.
Year names: each year was named after a major event ("the year of smiting the north"), the beginning of records like the Palermo Stone.
Counting wealth: a regular royal tour, the "following of Horus", was linked to assessing the land and its herds for taxes.
Royal titles: the king's Horus name in a serekh; by the reign of Den, the title nsw-bjt, "King of Upper and Lower Egypt".

blocks.html: The kings were buried at Abydos, in brick-lined pits with many rooms, and each had a big walled enclosure nearer the town. At Saqqara, overlooking Memphis, huge mud-brick tombs called mastabas (from the Arabic word for a bench) held the great officials of the court. In the 2nd Dynasty, King Peribsen put the god Seth instead of Horus above his name, and Khasekhemwy built a vast enclosure at Abydos; his reign leads into the age of stone.

blocks.title: Mud brick before stone
blocks.q: The first royal tombs are of mud brick and wood. The Step Pyramid, of stone, comes in the 3rd Dynasty. Which came first?
steps: Dynasties 1 and 2 are the Early Dynastic Period, c. 3000–2686 BC.
The Step Pyramid belongs to Djoser of the 3rd Dynasty, the start of the Old Kingdom.
So two dynasties of brick tombs came before any pyramid.
blocks.a: The brick tombs of Dynasties 1 and 2.

blocks.html: Thinking the pyramids came first. Two dynasties of mud-brick tombs, about three centuries of them, came before the first pyramid. A check: the Old Kingdom starts with the 3rd Dynasty; anything earlier is not a pyramid.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 4

blocks.html: The first dynasties built in mud brick. Then, at the start of the 3rd Dynasty, a king named Djoser (c. 2667–2648 BC) did something new: he had his tomb built entirely of cut stone, at Saqqara, high above Memphis.

Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara is the first large building made entirely of stone. Later Egyptians credited it to his official Imhotep. It did not start as a pyramid: it grew from a flat mastaba through several changes of plan into six steps, about 62 m high.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: The Step Pyramid of Djoser in profile: six stone steps, about 62 m high.

items: It began as a square, flat-topped stone mastaba.
The mastaba was enlarged twice.
Then the builders set smaller mastabas on top to make four steps.
Finally they enlarged it again into six steps.

blocks.html: A mastaba was the old shape of an important tomb. Stacking ever-smaller ones made the tomb taller and more visible, and may have reflected new ideas about the king rising to the sky. Each change shows builders trying something new with a material they were still learning to use: the stones are small, like stone versions of mud bricks.

Around the pyramid lay a huge walled enclosure with courtyards and dummy buildings of solid stone, including a court for the sed festival, the royal jubilee. Under the pyramid, shafts and tunnels lead to the burial chamber, and some rooms are lined with blue tiles that copy reed matting.

A statue base from the complex carries the name and titles of Imhotep, a high official of Djoser. Much later, Egyptians remembered him as the great architect and a wise man, and in the Late Period he was worshipped as a god of healing; Greeks linked him with their healer Asclepius. That a real official became a god shows how much later generations admired this achievement.

blocks.title: Telling the stages apart
blocks.q: A guide says the Step Pyramid was "designed as six steps from the start". What evidence shows otherwise?
steps: Inside and around the base, archaeologists can see earlier faces of stone covered by later additions.
These show a mastaba, then an enlarged mastaba, then four steps, then six.
So the building changed plan several times as it went.
blocks.a: The buried earlier faces of stone show the changes of plan.

blocks.html: Thinking the Step Pyramid was built as six steps from the start. It grew from a flat mastaba through several changes of plan. Check by asking what is hidden inside: the earlier stages are still there under the later ones.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 5, The Old Kingdom

blocks.html: After Djoser, later 3rd Dynasty kings began step pyramids too. The real leap came with Sneferu, first king of the 4th Dynasty (c. 2613–2589 BC). He built more stone than any other Egyptian king, and his builders learned, by trial and error, how to make a true pyramid with smooth, straight sides.

Sneferu built pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur: the Bent Pyramid, whose angle changes partway up, and the Red Pyramid, the first finished true pyramid. His son Khufu (c. 2589–2566 BC) built the Great Pyramid at Giza, and Khufu's successors Khafre and Menkaure built the other two Giza pyramids.

blocks.cap: Sneferu's two Dahshur pyramids and the three of Giza, side by side to scale.

blocks.html: A steeper pyramid puts more weight on the ground and on the rooms inside. At the Bent Pyramid, cracks and settling appeared, so the builders lowered the angle to reduce the load. For the Red Pyramid they used the gentler angle throughout. By Khufu's time they could build at about 52° on a carefully leveled platform of bedrock.

blocks.cap: The pyramid fields near Memphis: Giza, Abusir, Saqqara and Dahshur. Meidum lies farther south.

blocks.title: Which came first?
blocks.q: Put these in order: the Great Pyramid, the Bent Pyramid, the Step Pyramid.
steps: The Step Pyramid belongs to Djoser, 3rd Dynasty.
The Bent Pyramid belongs to Sneferu, first king of the 4th Dynasty.
The Great Pyramid belongs to Khufu, Sneferu's son.
blocks.a: Step Pyramid, Bent Pyramid, Great Pyramid.

blocks.html: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for almost 3,800 years. Inside are the Grand Gallery and the King's Chamber, lined with granite brought from Aswan, more than 800 km upriver.

Calling the Great Pyramid the first pyramid. Djoser's step pyramid came about a century earlier, and Sneferu built three pyramids before his son's. The Great Pyramid is the high point of a learning process, not its start.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 5

blocks.html: A pyramid like Khufu's needed stone, tools, boats, food and thousands of people, organized for twenty years or more. It is a monument to a king, and also to a state: the officials, scribes and work crews who could plan and run a project on that scale.

Pyramids needed an organized state: a vizier at the head of the government, scribes to keep accounts, taxes in grain and labor, quarries, boats and canals, and a workforce that was fed, housed and cared for. The evidence points to organized Egyptian crews, not huge gangs of slaves.

items: The workers' town: south of the Giza pyramids, excavations led by Mark Lehner uncovered bakeries, breweries, storerooms and barracks, with the bones of many cattle, sheep, goats and fish eaten there.

The workers' tombs: on the slope above the town, excavations led by Zahi Hawass found the tombs of overseers and workers, some with titles. Skeletons show hard labor and also healed fractures, a sign of medical care.
The crews' own names: work gangs painted names like "Friends of Khufu" on blocks.

The Diary of Merer: papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea, the oldest inscribed papyri known, are the logbook of an official named Merer whose crew carried limestone by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza late in Khufu's reign.

blocks.html: Grain was Egypt's wealth. The state collected it as tax and paid it out as rations of bread and beer. During the inundation, when the fields were under water, many farmers could be called up for state work. A permanent core of skilled builders worked all year, while larger rotating crews came and went.

blocks.cap: The Great Pyramid's passages and chambers, to scale (simplified).

blocks.text: What is known and what isn't

blocks.html: We know where the stone came from, how it was cut with copper tools and stone pounders, and that it was moved on sledges and boats. Exactly how the blocks were raised, by straight, zigzag or spiral ramps or some mix, is still debated. That is an honest gap in our knowledge, and archaeologists keep testing ideas against the remains.

blocks.title: Weighing a story
blocks.q: The Greek writer Herodotus, about two thousand years after Khufu, said 100,000 men labored in shifts on the Great Pyramid. How should a historian use this?
steps: Herodotus wrote long after the event and repeated what guides told him.
The excavated town, tombs and papyri are evidence from Khufu's own time.
Modern estimates from that evidence are in the tens of thousands at most, including people who baked, brewed and hauled.
blocks.a: As a late story to be tested against the archaeology, which points to a smaller, well-organized workforce.

blocks.html: Picturing huge gangs of slaves. The workers' town, bakeries, tombs and the Diary of Merer point to organized, fed Egyptian crews, some skilled and some called up for a season. Ideas that others (or a lost civilization) built the pyramids are rejected by archaeologists, because the builders left their town, tools, graves and records.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 5

blocks.html: After the giant pyramids of Giza, the kings of the 5th Dynasty (c. 2494–2345 BC) built smaller pyramids and put more of their wealth into something else: the cult of the sun god Ra.

Several 5th Dynasty kings built sun temples for Ra near Abusir, and royal names often included Ra (Sahure, Neferirkare, Niuserre). Unas, the last king of the dynasty (c. 2375–2345 BC), had the first Pyramid Texts, spells for the king's afterlife, carved on the walls inside his pyramid at Saqqara.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: From the Giza kings to Unas: about two centuries.

blocks.html: A sun temple was open to the sky. In its court stood a squat obelisk on a high base, a symbol of the sun, with a large altar in front of it. Only two have been found, at Abu Gurob near Abusir: Userkaf's and Niuserre's. Records name six. Their pyramids, at Abusir and Saqqara, were smaller and less solidly built than the Giza pyramids, but their temples were richly decorated with reliefs.

The king had always been linked with the gods; now his tie to Ra was stressed. Ra was the creator and the force that kept the world running each day, and the king, as "son of Ra", was his heir on earth. The title "son of Ra" became a regular part of the king's names around this time. You can read it in the royal titulary.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: zꜣ-rꜥ, "son of Ra": the pintail duck (zꜣ) and the sun (rꜥ).

blocks.html: Inside Unas's pyramid, columns of blue-painted hieroglyphs cover the walls of the burial chamber and antechamber. They are spells to protect the dead king and help him rise to join the sun god and the stars. Later kings and queens of the 6th Dynasty carved more spells in their pyramids. Some of the spells may be much older than Unas, but his is the first pyramid where they were written down. Records of temple business survive from this dynasty too, in the Abusir papyri.

blocks.title: Where are the texts?
blocks.q: A visitor expects to find Pyramid Texts inside the Great Pyramid of Khufu. Will she?
steps: Khufu belongs to the 4th Dynasty, c. 2589–2566 BC.
The Pyramid Texts begin with Unas, the last king of the 5th Dynasty, about two centuries later.
The Great Pyramid's chambers have no carved texts at all.
blocks.a: No. The Great Pyramid has no inscriptions inside; the texts begin with Unas.

blocks.html: Thinking the Pyramid Texts were carved in the Great Pyramid. The Great Pyramid has no inscriptions inside (only builders' marks in hidden spaces); the carved texts begin with Unas, about two centuries later. More on these texts in Religion, Art and Architecture.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 5

blocks.html: The 5th Dynasty ended with Unas, and the 6th Dynasty (c. 2345–2181 BC) began with Teti. Kings still built pyramids at Saqqara, and Egypt still sent expeditions to Nubia, Sinai and Byblos. But power was spreading out. Officials in the provinces grew richer and more independent, and some told the story of their careers in their tombs.

Under the 6th Dynasty, provincial governors (nomarchs) grew richer and more independent: their offices became hereditary and they built large tombs at home instead of near the king. Officials like Weni and Harkhuf left autobiographies describing their service.

items: Weni served Teti, Pepi I and Merenre. His autobiography, from his tomb chapel at Abydos, tells how he rose from a minor post to governor of Upper Egypt, led an army against "sand-dwellers" to the northeast, judged a case in the royal household, and fetched stone from distant quarries.

Harkhuf, governor of Elephantine at the southern border, led four trading expeditions into Nubia, to a land called Yam, returning with incense, ebony and ivory. On his tomb at Aswan he copied a letter from the young king Pepi II, delighted that Harkhuf was bringing back a dancer, and telling him to guard him well.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Weni's Abydos and Harkhuf's Elephantine. Harkhuf's journeys took him south beyond the First Cataract.

blocks.html: Running a long country from Memphis meant trusting governors far away. Kings rewarded them with land, titles and exemptions from tax. Over generations, families held the same office, kept the wealth at home, and owed more to their own nome than to the court. Autobiographies are part of that change: a man's own deeds, in his own tomb, in his own town.

These texts are wonderful sources, and they have an agenda: to present a perfect servant of the king, worthy of an afterlife. They tell what an official was proud of and how service was valued. They rarely mention failure. Read them as any other source: who wrote this, for whom, and why?

blocks.title: Reading a tomb
blocks.q: In the late Old Kingdom, more large tombs of high officials are built in provincial cemeteries rather than near the king's pyramid. What does that suggest?
steps: Where an official chose to be buried shows where his life and loyalties lay.
Earlier, great officials were buried near the king, whose favor gave them their place.
Burial at home suggests their power now rested in their own province.
blocks.a: Power was shifting from the court to the provinces.

blocks.html: Pepi II came to the throne as a child and is said to have reigned a very long time (Manetho says 94 years; many scholars think about 60 or a little more). His long reign leads into the end of the Old Kingdom.
Imagining that all power stayed with the king. Over time, the nome governors built their own power bases, with hereditary offices and local wealth. A check: look at where the big tombs are.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 5
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 1 (Chicago, 1906), the inscription of Uni (Weni) and the inscriptions of Harkhuf

blocks.html: After the 6th Dynasty, a series of short-lived kings at Memphis (the 7th and 8th Dynasties) ruled a shrinking realm, and by c. 2160 BC the Old Kingdom was over. Why did the age of the pyramids end? This is a real historical debate, and the evidence is incomplete.

Historians debate the causes. Proposed factors include a weaker central government as provincial governors grew powerful, the costs of tax exemptions for temples and royal cults, very long reigns and disputed successions, and perhaps low Nile floods and a drier climate. Most historians see several working together; they disagree about how much climate mattered.

blocks.html: Big historical changes rarely have one cause. A government already stretched by powerful provinces would be less able to cope with bad harvests; bad harvests would make people turn to local leaders who could feed them; a disputed succession would weaken the center further. Factors that are small alone can add up.

A governor of the First Intermediate Period, Ankhtifi, boasted in his tomb that all Upper Egypt was starving but he fed his people. Later literary texts describe the land turned upside down. Historians use these with care: a governor praising himself and a later poem with a message both have reasons to paint a dark picture.

blocks.title: Weighing a claim
blocks.q: A student writes: "The Old Kingdom fell because of a drought." What would make this a stronger historical argument?
steps: Name the evidence: climate data and Egyptian texts about famine.
Show the timing: did the dry phase come before the collapse, or after it?
Take account of other factors, such as the power of the nomarchs, and say how they worked together.
blocks.a: Presenting climate as one factor among several, with evidence and timing, not as the single cause.

blocks.html: Looking for a single cause. Most historians see several factors working together, and they disagree about the weight of each, especially climate. When you write about it, give the main positions and the evidence for each.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 6, The First Intermediate Period

blocks.html: When the Old Kingdom ended, no single king ruled the whole of Egypt for about a century. Historians call this the First Intermediate Period (c. 2160–2055 BC). It was a time of rival kings and strong local leaders, and also of real change in who could hope for a good afterlife.

After the Old Kingdom, rival dynasties ruled from Herakleopolis in the north (the 9th and 10th Dynasties) and Thebes in the south (the 11th Dynasty). Between them, local governors ran their own provinces and sometimes fought each other.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Herakleopolis (not marked) lay south of Memphis, near the mouth of the Faiyum; Thebes (Karnak) far to the south. The border between them shifted around Abydos.

South

blocks.html: Fighting centered on the borderlands around Abydos and Thinis. Local governors chose sides: Ankhtifi, who ruled two southern nomes from his base near Hierakonpolis, backed the north and fought the Thebans. His tomb tells of his deeds and of a famine in which, he says, he fed his people.

Without a strong king, the power that had already shifted to provincial governors in the late Old Kingdom came fully into the open. A governor who could defend his nome, store grain and feed his people earned their loyalty. Kings now needed allies among the governors to win.

Many provincial towns did well. Local workshops made their own styles of art, freed from the court's rules. And spells that had been only for kings, like the Pyramid Texts, began to be written inside the coffins of officials and their families. These Coffin Texts spread in the Middle Kingdom: a good afterlife was now hoped for by many more people.

blocks.title: Reading a later text
blocks.q: A Middle Kingdom literary text describes the time before as one when "the land was upside down". Does this prove the First Intermediate Period was a disaster everywhere?
steps: The text was written later, under kings who had reunited Egypt.
Those kings had reasons to describe the time before them as chaos that they ended.
Archaeology shows many local towns and cemeteries doing well in this period.
blocks.a: No. It is partly a message of the later kings; the evidence on the ground is more mixed.

blocks.html: Believing later texts that paint this time as total chaos. There was war and hardship in places, but also local prosperity and new ideas; the picture of disaster is partly propaganda of the Middle Kingdom kings who ended it.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 6, The First Intermediate Period

blocks.html: The First Intermediate Period ended with a southern victory. Mentuhotep II of Thebes came to the throne c. 2055 BC, and during his long reign (to c. 2004 BC) he defeated the kings of Herakleopolis and ruled the whole country again. Historians begin the Middle Kingdom with his reign.

Mentuhotep II of Thebes, a king of the 11th Dynasty, defeated the Herakleopolitan kings and reunited Egypt. The Middle Kingdom begins with his reign (c. 2055 BC), even though his dynasty had already been ruling in the south.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The 11th Dynasty begins in the First Intermediate Period at Thebes and continues into the Middle Kingdom.

blocks.html: A period label marks a change in the state, not in the family. The 11th Dynasty began as one of two rival houses. When one of its kings ruled all of Egypt again, the historical situation changed, so historians start a new period with him while keeping Manetho's dynasty number. That is why the 11th Dynasty appears in two periods.

Mentuhotep II changed his Horus name more than once during his reign. One of his later names, Sematawy, means "he who unites the Two Lands", which suggests the reunion came partway through his reign. Tombs at Thebes hold soldiers who seem to have died in battle, and inscriptions of his officials tell of campaigns. Later Egyptians remembered him as the founder of a new age.

Mentuhotep II built a new kind of royal tomb and temple at Deir el-Bahari, in a bay of the cliffs on the west bank at Thebes: terraces, colonnades and a central building, with his tomb cut deep into the rock behind. About five centuries later, Hatshepsut built her own terraced temple right beside it, perhaps inspired by it.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Deir el-Bahari on the west bank at Thebes, where Mentuhotep II's temple stands beside Hatshepsut's.

blocks.title: Which dynasty, which period?
blocks.q: Mentuhotep II's father, also an 11th Dynasty king, ruled only the south. In which period did the father reign, and in which period did Mentuhotep II's reunited reign fall?
steps: Before the reunion, Egypt was divided: that is the First Intermediate Period.
Mentuhotep II's reign is where historians start the Middle Kingdom.
Both kings belong to the 11th Dynasty.
blocks.a: The father: the First Intermediate Period. Mentuhotep II: the start of the Middle Kingdom. Same dynasty, different periods.

blocks.html: Expecting a new kingdom to start with a new dynasty. Mentuhotep II was already a king of the 11th Dynasty; the period changes because Egypt became one state again, not because a new family took over.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 7, The Middle Kingdom Renaissance

blocks.html: The 11th Dynasty of Mentuhotep II did not last long after him. Its last king's vizier was a man named Amenemhat, and most historians think this vizier became Amenemhat I, founder of the 12th Dynasty (c. 1985–1773 BC). Its kings ruled for about two centuries, one of the most stable stretches in Egyptian history.

Amenemhat I founded the 12th Dynasty and a new capital, Itjtawy, near el-Lisht, between Memphis and the Faiyum. Its kings, named Amenemhat and Senusret, ruled about two centuries and built pyramids again.
