blocks.html: Moving the capital north, near the meeting point of the valley and the Delta, put the king close to the old center of power at Memphis and to the routes to the north. The name says it all: Itjtawy means "(Amenemhat is) the one who seizes the Two Lands".

blocks.text: Keeping the throne in the family

blocks.html: Amenemhat I was killed in a palace conspiracy, as two famous texts, the Teaching of Amenemhat and the Tale of Sinuhe, tell. Several 12th Dynasty kings seem to have made their sons co-rulers before they died, so that the heir already held power. How long these co-regencies lasted, and even whether some of them happened, is still discussed.

blocks.title: Sorting the names
blocks.q: A student mixes up "the Senusret who built forts at the Second Cataract" and "the Senusret of the White Chapel". Which numbers are they?
steps: Senusret I built the White Chapel at Karnak and pushed into Nubia.
Senusret III built the great chain of forts at the Second Cataract.
Tie each number to a deed, and the names stop blurring.
blocks.a: The White Chapel: Senusret I. The chain of forts: Senusret III.

blocks.html: Mixing up the repeated names. Greek writers called these kings Ammenemes and Sesostris, and both names repeat. Number them and attach one deed to each: Senusret I (White Chapel), Senusret III (forts), Amenemhat III (Faiyum and Hawara).

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 7

blocks.html: Among the 12th Dynasty kings, Senusret III (c. 1870–1831 BC) left one of the deepest marks. Later Egyptians remembered him as a great conqueror and honored him as a god in Nubia. His statues show a careworn, heavy-lidded face, unlike the calm, youthful faces of earlier kings.
Senusret III built a chain of forts at the Second Cataract, fixed the southern border at Semna with an inscribed stela, and his reign saw the great provincial governors lose their old independence.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The First Cataract at Aswan and, far to the south, the Second Cataract with the forts of Buhen and Semna. Kerma lay beyond, in Kush.

blocks.html: Middle Kingdom builders lined the rocky Second Cataract with massive mud-brick forts: Buhen, Mirgissa, Semna, Kumma and others, with thick walls, towers, ditches and gates. Some were begun earlier, under Senusret I; Senusret III added more and fixed the frontier. The forts guarded the river, watched the desert and controlled trade with Kush, whose kingdom was centered at Kerma. Most of these forts now lie under Lake Nasser.

The Second Cataract is a natural choke point: boats must slow down and be hauled through, so a few forts could control everything that moved on the river. Gold, ivory, ebony and incense came from the south, and holding the cataract let Egypt control that trade.

In his Year 8, Senusret III set up a boundary stela at Semna. It says no Nubian may pass north by water or by land, except to trade or on official business. A second stela, of his Year 16, praises any son of his who holds the border and tells of a statue of the king set up there, so the border was guarded by his image as well as his soldiers.

Around his reign, the great tombs of provincial governors, like those at Beni Hasan, stop being built, and the government seems to have been reorganized into large departments run from the capital. Many historians think Senusret III curbed the governors' power; others think the change was more gradual. Either way, the court was stronger at the end.

blocks.title: Where was the border?
blocks.q: In the Old Kingdom, Egypt's usual southern border was at the First Cataract (Aswan). Where was it under Senusret III?
steps: The forts and the boundary stela stand at the Second Cataract.
The Second Cataract is more than 300 km south of the First.
So the border had moved far south, deep into Lower Nubia.
blocks.a: At Semna, by the Second Cataract.

blocks.html: Placing Egypt's border at Aswan for all of history. In the Middle Kingdom Egypt pushed south to the Second Cataract, and in the New Kingdom farther still. The border moved with Egypt's power.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 7
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 1 (Chicago, 1906), the Semna stelae of Senusret III

blocks.html: The Middle Kingdom was the classic age of Egyptian writing. Its language, Middle Egyptian, became the model that scribes copied and studied for the rest of Egyptian history, rather as later Europeans studied Latin. Its stories and teachings were read for a thousand years.

The Middle Kingdom was the classic age of Egyptian literature: stories like the Tale of Sinuhe and the Eloquent Peasant, and teaching texts (wisdom literature) that give advice on how to live, all written in Middle Egyptian.

head: Work
Kind
What it is about
rows: an official flees Egypt when Amenemhat I is killed, lives in the Levant, and comes home in old age to be buried in Egypt
a farmer robbed on the road pleads for justice in nine beautiful speeches
a sailor cast away on a magical island meets a giant serpent
advice from an old vizier to his son: listen, be modest, speak well
a father praises the scribe's life over every other trade, with comic pictures of other jobs
blocks.cap: Some Middle Kingdom literature.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: sḏm, "hear, listen". Teaching texts again and again call on the reader to listen.

blocks.html: Literature needs readers and writers with time and training. The strong, settled state of the 12th Dynasty trained many scribes, and the elite who ran the country valued fine speech and wise conduct. Stories and teachings expressed and taught those values, which is one reason later schools kept copying them.

Some Middle Kingdom papyri survive, but many works are known from New Kingdom copies: schoolboys and scribes copied passages of Sinuhe and the teachings on papyri and on ostraca, flakes of limestone. That is strong evidence that these texts were classics, studied centuries after they were written.

blocks.title: Why copy old texts?
blocks.q: Pieces of the Tale of Sinuhe were copied by New Kingdom scribes, about five hundred years after it was composed. What does that tell us?
steps: People do not copy texts for centuries unless they value them.
Copying was also how scribes learned to write and to use the classical language.
So Sinuhe had become a classic, part of a scribe's education.
blocks.a: That it was a classic, studied and copied in school.

blocks.html: Middle Egyptian stayed the language of formal inscriptions long after people stopped speaking it. If you study it in Middle Egyptian I, you will read the same language as Sinuhe.
Thinking Egyptian writing was only religious or royal. Middle Kingdom scribes also wrote stories, poems, letters and advice. Check: the Eloquent Peasant is about a farmer, not a king or a god.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 7

blocks.html: After the 12th Dynasty, the many short-lived kings of the 13th Dynasty still held much of Egypt for a time. In the eastern Delta, though, people from western Asia had been settling for generations. Around c. 1650 BC, rulers from among them took power over the north. Egyptians called them ḥqꜣw ḫꜣswt, "rulers of foreign lands", which Greek writers turned into Hyksos.

The Hyksos, rulers of western Asian origin, governed northern Egypt from Avaris in the eastern Delta as the 15th Dynasty (c. 1650–1550 BC). They took over Egyptian royal titles and writing, while Theban kings ruled the south.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḥqꜣ, "ruler", and ḫꜣst, "foreign land". The Hyksos were the ḥqꜣw ḫꜣswt, "rulers of foreign lands" (both words in the plural).

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Avaris (Tell el-Dabʿa) in the eastern Delta, on the road to the Levant.

blocks.html: Since 1966 Manfred Bietak's excavations at Tell el-Dabʿa, ancient Avaris, have shown a town where people with Levantine customs lived from the late Middle Kingdom on: houses of Near Eastern type, Middle Bronze Age pottery and weapons, and burials with donkeys. The town grew over generations before the Hyksos kings ruled from it.

blocks.text: How did they come to power?

blocks.html: Here historians disagree. Manetho, quoted by Josephus centuries later, describes a sudden invasion. Many scholars now think of a gradual rise: settlers, traders and soldiers in the Delta whose leaders took power when the 13th Dynasty weakened, perhaps with some fighting. Others think new groups arriving from the Levant played a bigger part. The evidence fits a long presence, with the exact way power changed hands still debated.

Avaris lay where the land route from the Levant entered Egypt. A border town is a place of trade and mixing; over generations its people became part of Egyptian life while keeping their own customs. When central power weakened, the leaders of such a rich, well-connected town could rule the region.

blocks.title: A sign of Egyptian culture
blocks.q: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, a famous Egyptian math text, was copied in Year 33 of the Hyksos king Apepi. What does that suggest about Hyksos rule?
steps: The papyrus is written in Egyptian hieratic and dated by a Hyksos king's reign.
So Egyptian scribes worked under the Hyksos and dated their work by them.
Hyksos rulers used Egyptian administration and culture rather than replacing it.
blocks.a: That Egyptian scribal culture continued under Hyksos kings, who were treated as rulers of Egypt.

blocks.html: New things came into Egypt in this period too: horses and chariots, and new kinds of weapons, which the New Kingdom army would use to great effect.

Picturing a sudden invasion by a horde. Archaeology shows people from western Asia living in the Delta for generations before Hyksos kings took power; how they took it is debated. Avoid "barbarian" language, which comes from later Egyptian propaganda.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 8, The Second Intermediate Period

blocks.html: While the Hyksos ruled the north of Egypt, another power was rising in the south. Beyond the Second Cataract forts, the kingdom of Kush, centered at Kerma near the Third Cataract, had grown into one of the strongest states in Africa.

The kingdom of Kush, with its capital at Kerma, grew strong during the Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate Period. It took over the Egyptian forts in Lower Nubia and was allied with the Hyksos against Thebes.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Kerma, south of the Third Cataract, and the Egyptian forts it took over at the Second Cataract.

blocks.text: A kingdom with its own culture

items: The city: Kerma had a huge mud-brick temple, the Western Deffufa, still standing about 18 m high, with houses, workshops and a palace around it.
Royal tombs: its kings were buried under great round mounds, some about 90 m across, with rich goods.
Craft: Kerma potters made thin, polished black-topped beakers of remarkable quality.
Excavation: George Reisner dug there in 1913–16; since the 1970s Charles Bonnet and colleagues have studied the city.

blocks.html: Kush controlled the river route south and the gold of the Nubian deserts. That wealth, and its position between Egypt and the lands farther south, made it both Egypt's trading partner and its rival. When Egypt was strong, it built forts against Kush; when Egypt was divided, Kush pushed north.

In the Theban war, King Kamose of Thebes set up stelae at Karnak. One tells how his men caught a messenger on the desert road carrying a letter from the Hyksos king Apepi to the new ruler of Kush, asking him to attack Thebes from the south while the Hyksos held the north. Thebes was caught between two allies. An inscription in a tomb at Elkab also tells of a raid by Kush and its allies deep into Upper Egypt.

blocks.title: Why an alliance?
blocks.q: Why would the Hyksos king want an alliance with Kush?
steps: Thebes lay between the Hyksos in the north and Kush in the south.
An attack from both sides would split Theban forces.
So the two powers had a shared interest in keeping Thebes weak.
blocks.a: To trap Thebes between them.

blocks.html: Early in the New Kingdom, Egypt struck back: Thutmose I campaigned far into Kush and broke the power of Kerma. Later Kushite kingdoms, at Napata and Meroë, carried on Nubia's own history.

Seeing Nubia only as Egypt's colony. Kerma was a powerful kingdom with its own culture, kings and art, and for a time it was strong enough to threaten Egypt. Egyptian texts call Kush "wretched", which tells us about Egyptian propaganda, not about Kush.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 8

blocks.html: By about c. 1580 BC, the Theban kings of the 17th Dynasty held Upper Egypt, with the Hyksos in the north and Kush to the south. Over about a generation, three Theban kings fought to take back the whole country.

Theban kings Seqenenre Tao and Kamose fought the Hyksos, and Ahmose took Avaris and drove them out (c. 1550 BC), then pursued them into southern Canaan. His reign begins the New Kingdom and the 18th Dynasty.

head: King
What the sources say
rows: his mummy shows terrible head wounds, probably from battle; a much later story tells of a quarrel between him and the Hyksos king
his stelae at Karnak describe sailing north, attacking Hyksos allies and reaching Avaris, and intercepting the letter to Kush
besieged and took Avaris, then besieged Sharuhen in southern Canaan; campaigned in Nubia
blocks.cap: Three kings of the war.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The end of the Second Intermediate Period and the start of the New Kingdom.

blocks.html: One of the best sources is the tomb of Ahmose son of Ebana, a soldier from Elkab who served in the navy under King Ahmose and later kings. In his tomb autobiography he lists his battles at Avaris and Sharuhen and the rewards he received, gold and captives. It is a rare look at the war from the deck of a ship.

The Thebans had a base in the south and the old prestige of the Middle Kingdom kings. They also had a reason to fight: the war could reunite Egypt under Theban rule. Each king pushed farther north than the last. Women of the royal family were important too: a stela of King Ahmose praises his mother, Queen Ahhotep, for caring for the army and rallying Upper Egypt.

blocks.title: How long did it take?
blocks.q: Seqenenre Tao, Kamose and Ahmose each fought the Hyksos. Why does that show the war was not quick?
steps: Each king came to the throne after the one before died.
Seqenenre died, probably in battle; Kamose reigned only a few years; Ahmose finished the war.
Three reigns of fighting means a war lasting years, not one battle.
blocks.a: It took at least three kings, over years of fighting.

blocks.html: With Avaris taken, Egypt was one country again. Ahmose founded the New Kingdom, and the experience of war made the new state more military than any before it.
Thinking the war was quick. It took at least three Theban kings, with sieges of Avaris and of Sharuhen, and the Theban side took losses too. A check: count the kings who fought it.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 8
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (Chicago, 1906), the biography of Ahmose son of Ebana

blocks.html: The Theban war left Egypt united and battle-hardened. Ahmose (c. 1550–1525 BC) founded the 18th Dynasty and the New Kingdom, and over the next century his successors carried Egyptian armies farther than ever before: north into the Levant and south deep into Nubia.

Ahmose founded the 18th Dynasty; his successors, above all Thutmose I and Thutmose III, pushed into the Levant and Nubia and built an empire: vassal kingdoms in Canaan and Syria, and Egyptian rule over Nubia under a viceroy.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The reach of the New Kingdom empire: from the Levant to the Fourth Cataract.

head: The Levant (north)
Nubia (south)
rows: local kings as vassals, with Egyptian garrisons and officials in some towns
directly, by a viceroy called the "King's Son of Kush"
tribute, trade routes, a buffer against rival empires
gold, ivory, ebony, cattle and soldiers
the kingdom of Kush at Kerma, defeated early in the dynasty
princes of vassal kings raised at the Egyptian court
Egyptian temples and towns along the Nile
blocks.cap: How Egypt ran its empire.

blocks.html: The Hyksos had shown that a threat could come from the northeast. Holding the Levant kept enemies far from the Delta, and it gave Egypt control of rich trade routes. In the south, Nubia had the gold that paid for temples, armies and diplomacy. Victory also brought wealth to the god Amun of Thebes, whose temple at Karnak grew enormously.

items: Ahmose drove out the Hyksos and campaigned in Canaan and Nubia.
Amenhotep I consolidated the state; later the workmen of Deir el-Medina honored him as their patron.
Thutmose I marched to the Euphrates in the north and far past the Fourth Cataract in the south, and was probably the first king buried in the Valley of the Kings.
Thutmose III, after the reign of Hatshepsut, fought campaign after campaign and made Egypt the leading power of the region.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The New Kingdom: the empire was built in the first century of the 18th Dynasty.

blocks.title: When was the empire built?
blocks.q: A student says, "Ramesses II built Egypt's empire." Using the timeline, what is wrong with that?
steps: Thutmose I and Thutmose III campaigned in the Levant and Nubia c. 1504–1425 BC.
Ramesses II reigned c. 1279–1213 BC, about two centuries later.
He fought to keep and restore parts of an empire that already existed.
blocks.a: The empire was built mostly by the early 18th Dynasty kings; Ramesses II defended it.

blocks.html: Dating the empire to Ramesses II. He is the most famous New Kingdom king, but the empire was built mostly by the early 18th Dynasty, especially Thutmose I and Thutmose III. A check: look at who first reached the Euphrates.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9, The 18th Dynasty before the Amarna Period

blocks.html: When Thutmose II died, his son Thutmose III was a small child. The boy's stepmother and aunt, Hatshepsut, daughter of Thutmose I and widow of Thutmose II, acted as regent. Within a few years she did something unprecedented in scale: she took the full titles of a king and ruled as king herself, beside the young Thutmose.
Hatshepsut ruled first as regent for Thutmose III and then as king (c. 1473–1458 BC). She built at Karnak and her great temple at Deir el-Bahari, and sent a famous expedition to Punt.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Hatshepsut's reign sits inside the long reign of Thutmose III, who counted his years from c. 1479 BC.

blocks.html: Egyptian kingship was a male office, but a few women had held it before, such as Sobekneferu at the end of the 12th Dynasty. Hatshepsut took a throne name, Maatkare, and was shown with the king's kilt, crown and false beard, while her inscriptions often keep feminine word endings. She claimed that the god Amun was her true father, and reliefs at her temple tell the story of her divine birth.

Kingship was the keystone of the Egyptian order: the king offered to the gods and kept maat. A regent could manage affairs, but only a king could perform the king's role. By becoming king, with Amun's backing, Hatshepsut gave herself full authority, and Thutmose III remained king beside her.

items: Deir el-Bahari: her temple Djeser-djeseru ("holiest of holy places"), with three terraces against the cliffs, next to Mentuhotep II's older temple.
Karnak: a pair of great obelisks (one still stands) and the Red Chapel for Amun's sacred boat.
Punt: reliefs at Deir el-Bahari show ships bringing incense trees, ebony and animals from Punt, a land somewhere on the African coast of the Red Sea (its exact location is debated).

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Deir el-Bahari across the river from Karnak.

blocks.html: After her death, Thutmose III ruled alone for about thirty years. Late in his reign, about twenty years after she died, her images and names were cut out of many monuments and her statues broken. Because this came so late, most historians no longer think it was an act of personal hatred. A common view is that it removed a female king from the record and secured the succession for Thutmose's son; the reasons are still debated.

blocks.title: Reading the timing
blocks.q: If the erasure of Hatshepsut's images had been revenge, when would you expect it to happen? When did it happen?
steps: Revenge would most likely come right after she died, around c. 1458 BC.
The evidence shows the erasure late in Thutmose III's reign, about two decades later.
That timing points to a political motive, such as the succession, rather than anger.
blocks.a: Revenge would be early; the erasure came late, which suggests a political reason.

blocks.html: Repeating that her images were destroyed right after her death in anger. Most were removed late in Thutmose III's reign, perhaps for reasons of succession. The timing is the key evidence.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9

blocks.html: Once Hatshepsut was gone, Thutmose III (reigned c. 1479–1425 BC) led his army north almost every year. His first campaign, in his Year 23, ended in one of the best-documented battles of the ancient world.

Thutmose III won the battle of Megiddo (c. 1457 BC) against a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian rulers led by the king of Kadesh, and then led many campaigns into the Levant, reaching the Euphrates. Egypt became the leading power of the region.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Megiddo guarded a pass on the main road north through Canaan; Kadesh lay far to the north.

blocks.html: The account of the campaign, carved at Karnak in Thutmose's Annals, tells how the army reached the ridge south of Megiddo. Three roads led over it. His officers urged the two wide roads around; the king chose the narrow Aruna pass, straight through, where the army had to march in single file. The enemy, expecting him elsewhere, was caught off guard. The coalition broke and fled into Megiddo, and after a long siege the city surrendered.

Megiddo sat where the great road from Egypt to Syria crossed into the Jezreel Valley. Whoever held it controlled traffic between Egypt and the north. Defeating a coalition there, with the king of Kadesh at its head, broke organized resistance in Canaan for years.

items: The Annals, on the walls around Karnak's sanctuary, record campaigns, booty and tribute year by year, based on a daybook kept by army scribes.
In about his Year 33 his army crossed the Euphrates, with boats carried overland, and set up a stela next to that of his grandfather Thutmose I.
Sons of defeated rulers were brought to Egypt and raised at court, then sent home as loyal vassals.
Karnak received much of the wealth; his Festival Hall there even has reliefs of plants and animals seen on campaign.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Megiddo and Kadesh, almost two centuries apart.

blocks.title: Megiddo or Kadesh?
blocks.q: Which battle goes with which king: Megiddo (c. 1457 BC) and Kadesh (c. 1274 BC)?
steps: Megiddo came early in the 18th Dynasty empire: Thutmose III's first campaign.
Kadesh came about 180 years later, in the 19th Dynasty: Ramesses II against the Hittites.
Memory aid: the earlier battle belongs to the earlier king.
blocks.a: Megiddo: Thutmose III. Kadesh: Ramesses II.

blocks.html: Mixing up Megiddo (Thutmose III, a clear Egyptian victory over a Canaanite coalition) and Kadesh (Ramesses II, a draw with the Hittite empire). Kadesh was also the city whose king led the coalition at Megiddo, which adds to the confusion.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (Chicago, 1906), the Annals of Thutmose III

blocks.html: A few generations after Thutmose III, his great-grandson Amenhotep III (c. 1390–1352 BC) inherited an empire at peace. His reign of nearly forty years was one of the richest in Egyptian history: vast temples, colossal statues, splendid festivals, and gifts of gold flowing out to foreign courts.

Amenhotep III ruled a rich and peaceful empire. Letters between his court and the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Assyria, the Hittites and others, and from his vassals in Canaan, survive in the Amarna letters: clay tablets written in Akkadian cuneiform, the diplomatic language of the day.

items: The core of Luxor Temple, for Amun.
A huge memorial temple on the west bank at Thebes, of which the two Colossi of Memnon still stand.
A palace city at Malkata, on the west bank, with a great artificial harbor.
Large commemorative scarabs announcing events such as his marriage to Queen Tiye and his hunts.

blocks.html: In 1887 a local woman digging at Amarna found a cache of clay tablets. About 380 are now known. They come from the archive of the foreign office at Akhetaten, the city of Akhenaten, and cover the last years of Amenhotep III and the reign of his son. They are written in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped script of Mesopotamia, and mostly in Akkadian, which scribes across the Near East learned for diplomacy.

head: Writer
Kind of letter
rows: letters between "brothers": gifts, marriages, complaints about too little gold
The kings of Assyria and Hatti
new powers seeking recognition as equals
Rulers of Canaanite towns (Byblos, Jerusalem and others)
vassals reporting to "the king, my lord", often asking for troops and accusing their neighbors
blocks.cap: Who wrote the Amarna letters.

blocks.html: Great kings dealt with each other as a family of equals, calling each other "brother", exchanging princesses and luxury gifts. Egypt's gold was its strongest card: foreign kings asked for it again and again. Akkadian was the shared language, as French was the language of European diplomacy centuries later.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: The birth name Amenhotep (jmn-ḥtp, "Amun is content"). Amun's name is written first out of honor.

blocks.title: What language?
blocks.q: A museum label says an Amarna letter is "written in hieroglyphs". Why is that wrong?
steps: The letters are on clay tablets, pressed with a stylus.
Their script is cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks, not hieroglyphs.
Their language is mostly Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the time.
blocks.a: They are in Akkadian cuneiform on clay, not Egyptian hieroglyphs.

blocks.html: Thinking the Amarna letters were written in Egyptian. They are clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform, even the letters Egypt's own scribes wrote. Check: hieroglyphs are pictures; cuneiform is wedges.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9

blocks.html: Amenhotep III's son came to the throne as Amenhotep IV (c. 1352 BC). Within five years he had changed his name, his capital and the religion of the state. Few reigns in Egyptian history are so much studied and so much argued about.

Akhenaten made the Aten, the disk of the sun, the center of worship, closed or neglected the temples of other gods, had the name of Amun cut out of monuments, and built a new capital at Amarna (Akhetaten, "Horizon of the Aten").

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Amarna in Middle Egypt, about halfway between Memphis and Thebes, on land not sacred to any other god.

items: The name: Amenhotep ("Amun is content") became Akhenaten, often explained as "effective for the Aten".
The god: the Aten was shown as a sun disk whose rays end in hands, some holding the sign of life to the king and queen.
The city: Akhetaten was built quickly on empty land, marked out by boundary stelae.
Other gods: Amun's name and images were hacked out; temples lost support.
Art: royal figures were shown in a new style, with long faces and curving bodies, and in intimate family scenes.

blocks.html: The sun had always been central to Egyptian religion, and the Aten was already honored under Amenhotep III. Akhenaten went much further, putting one divine power above and in place of the others. Historians still discuss his motives: religious conviction, a wish to reduce the power of Amun's priesthood, or both.

Some scholars call Akhenaten's religion the first monotheism, worship of a single god. Others object. The Aten could be approached through the king and his family: people prayed to the royal family, and the king called himself the only one who truly knew the Aten. Some older gods were still tolerated for a while. So scholars debate whether "monotheism" is the right word, and many prefer to describe it in its own terms. The Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in a tomb at Amarna, shows its vision: one sun god who creates and sustains every land and creature.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The Amarna Period: Akhenaten's reign and the years after it.

blocks.title: Reading the evidence
blocks.q: At Amarna, people kept small shrines with images of the royal family worshipping the Aten. What does that suggest?
steps: Ordinary people were not shown worshipping the Aten directly.
Instead they honored the king and queen, who worshipped the Aten.
So the king stood between the god and the people, a point in the monotheism debate.
blocks.a: The royal family acted as the link between the Aten and everyone else.

blocks.html: Calling Akhenaten's religion simple monotheism. Scholars debate the word: the king himself held a special place between the Aten and the people, and the change did not outlast him. Present it as a debate, with both views.
Amarna art and its meaning are explored in Religion, Art and Architecture.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10, The Amarna Period and the Later New Kingdom

blocks.html: Akhenaten died c. 1336 BC. After a short reign or two, a boy of about eight or nine came to the throne as Tutankhaten, "living image of the Aten". Within a few years he had become Tutankhamun, "living image of Amun", and the old religion was back.

Tutankhamun (c. 1336–1327 BC), Ay and Horemheb brought back the old gods, left Amarna and restored the temples. Later kings treated the Amarna kings as illegitimate and left them out of their king lists.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn, "living image of Amun". The name of Amun is written first out of honor, but read last.

blocks.html: A stela set up at Karnak in Tutankhamun's name describes the land he inherited: temples abandoned from Elephantine to the Delta, their shrines in ruins and overgrown, and the gods turning away from Egypt. It then lists the king's works: new cult images, priests appointed, temple estates restored. It is official propaganda, painting the time before as a disaster, but it shows plainly what the new government wanted to be seen doing.

items: Tutankhamun was a boy, and officials governed for him: the courtier Ay and the general Horemheb.
The court moved back to Memphis; Akhetaten was abandoned.
Tutankhamun died at about eighteen or nineteen. Ay became king for a few years, then Horemheb (c. 1323–1295 BC).
Horemheb pulled down Akhenaten's buildings and reused their blocks as fill inside new pylons at Karnak.

blocks.html: Rejecting Akhenaten meant more than reopening temples. If the Amarna kings were rulers against maat, they should not be among the honored ancestors. The Abydos list goes straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb, and one later legal text dates an event to "Year 59 of Horemheb", counting the Amarna years as if they were his.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: From Akhenaten to Seti I. The later lists jump from Amenhotep III to Horemheb.

blocks.title: Why is Tutankhamun famous?
blocks.q: Tutankhamun reigned about nine years and died young. Why is he the best-known Egyptian king today?
steps: In 1922 Howard Carter found his tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV62, almost intact.
Most royal tombs had been robbed in antiquity; his treasures survived.
His fame comes from his tomb, not from his reign.
blocks.a: Because his nearly intact tomb was found in 1922.

blocks.html: Thinking Tutankhamun was a great ruler. He was a young king whose fame comes from his tomb. The stronger figures of these years were Ay and above all Horemheb.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10

blocks.html: Horemheb, the last king of the 18th Dynasty, had no son. He chose an army officer from the eastern Delta, who became Ramesses I and founded the 19th Dynasty. His grandson, Ramesses II, became the most famous builder in Egyptian history.

Ramesses II of the 19th Dynasty reigned about 66 years (c. 1279–1213 BC). He built more than any other king, including Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, and moved his capital to Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: rꜥ-ms-sw, "Ra is the one who bore him": the sun, the three fox skins (ms) and the folded cloth (s). Champollion read this name in 1822.

blocks.html: A capital in the eastern Delta put the king near his family's home and near the road to the Levant, where the army had to face the Hittites. Colossal statues and temples across the land, from the Delta to Nubia, showed one king everywhere: a message of power aimed at Egyptians, Nubians and foreigners alike.

Ramesses II also carved his cartouches on monuments built by earlier kings, sometimes cutting out their names. Egyptologists call this usurpation. So a statue or a temple wall with his name is not always his work: style, earlier traces and other evidence must decide. Greek writers knew him as Ozymandias, from his throne name, User-maat-ra.

blocks.title: Whose statue?
blocks.q: A statue in the style of the Middle Kingdom carries the cartouche of Ramesses II, carved more deeply than the rest of the inscription. What is the likely story?
steps: The style belongs to a period about seven centuries before Ramesses II.
A recut, deeper inscription suggests an older name was removed and replaced.
So Ramesses probably took over an older statue.
blocks.a: An older statue, usurped by Ramesses II.

blocks.html: Crediting Ramesses with every monument bearing his name. He also carved his name on older buildings and statues. Check the style and look for traces of an earlier name.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10

blocks.html: In his Year 5 (c. 1274 BC), Ramesses II marched north to fight the Hittites, the great empire of Anatolia, for control of Syria. The armies met at the city of Kadesh on the Orontes River. Ramesses told the story of the battle on more temple walls than any other event of his reign.

At Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) Ramesses II fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II to a draw. Years later, in his Year 21 (c. 1259 BC), Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III made a peace treaty, one of the earliest known.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Kadesh on the Orontes, at the edge of the Hittite sphere.

blocks.text: The battle, as Ramesses told it

items: The army marched in four divisions named for gods: Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth.
Two captured nomads said the Hittites were far to the north. It was a trick.
The Hittite chariots struck the division of Ra on the march and then the king's camp.
In Ramesses' account he fought almost alone, the god Amun at his side, until fresh troops arrived and drove the Hittites back.

blocks.html: The temple version, in a long poem and a shorter report with reliefs, was made to show the king as the hero who saved the day with Amun's help. That is what royal inscriptions were for. Historians compare it with what happened next: Kadesh stayed Hittite, the region of Amurru went back to the Hittite side, and Ramesses never took Kadesh.

About sixteen years later, with Assyria rising, both powers made peace. The treaty survives in two versions: an Egyptian text carved at Karnak and the Ramesseum, and a Hittite version in Akkadian on clay tablets found at Hattusa, the Hittite capital. Each side promised not to attack the other, to help against enemies and to return fugitives. Later Ramesses married a Hittite princess. A copy of the treaty hangs at the United Nations headquarters in New York.

blocks.title: Win, lose or draw?
blocks.q: Ramesses' temples call Kadesh a victory. Afterward, the Hittites still held Kadesh, and Egypt's northern border did not move. What is the best description of the outcome?
steps: A victory usually leaves the winner holding the prize.
Here the Hittites kept the city and the region.
But the Egyptian army survived and withdrew in order.
blocks.a: A draw at best for Egypt, presented at home as a victory.

blocks.html: Reading Ramesses' temple reliefs as proof of a great victory. Hittite records and the outcome suggest a draw. Use the rule for royal inscriptions: kings recorded victories.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 3 (Chicago, 1906), the battle of Kadesh

blocks.html: By the early 12th century BC, the eastern Mediterranean was in turmoil. Cities in the Levant and Anatolia were destroyed, the Hittite empire fell apart, and groups of people on the move, by land and sea, threatened Egypt. Ramesses III (c. 1184–1153 BC), the greatest king of the 20th Dynasty, met them in battle.

Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples in his Year 8 and Libyan invaders in other years, recording his wars at Medinet Habu. Late in his reign came the first known strike: the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina stopped work because their rations were late.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Medinet Habu, Ramesses III's memorial temple, and the workmen's village of Deir el-Medina nearby.

blocks.html: The Medinet Habu reliefs show a land battle and a sea battle at the edge of the Delta, with warriors in feathered and horned helmets, ox carts with women and children, and ships with bird-headed prows. The texts name groups such as the Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh. Most scholars identify the Peleset with the Philistines, who settled on the coast of Canaan. Earlier, Merneptah had fought some of these groups too, allied with Libyans.

Where did they come from? Here scholars disagree. Some point to the Aegean world, others to western Anatolia, Cyprus or even Sardinia and Sicily, from the similarity of names like Sherden and Shekelesh. Many see them not as one nation but as a mix of groups uprooted by the collapse of the Late Bronze Age kingdoms, through war, drought or famine. Their origins remain debated.

In Year 29 of Ramesses III, the workmen who cut the royal tombs walked off the job and sat down behind the temples, saying "We are hungry", because their monthly grain rations were weeks late. A papyrus now in Turin, kept by the village scribe Amennakht, records it. Officials brought rations and the men went back, but the protests happened again. It shows the strains on the state, and the workers' sense that they had a right to be paid.

items: Papyrus Harris I, made at the end of his reign, lists his huge gifts to the temples.
A plot in the royal household against the king was put on trial; the court records survive.

blocks.title: One nation?
blocks.q: The reliefs at Medinet Habu name at least five groups among the attackers. What does that suggest?
steps: Egyptian scribes gave each group its own name.
Different groups came with different gear and helmets.
So the "Sea Peoples" were a coalition or a movement of many groups, not one nation.
blocks.a: A mix of groups, whose origins are debated.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sea Peoples were one nation. They were a mix of groups on the move, and where each came from is debated. The name "Sea Peoples" itself is modern, made up in the 1800s.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (Chicago, 1906), the Medinet Habu inscriptions of Ramesses III

blocks.html: After Ramesses III, eight more kings named Ramesses ruled until c. 1069 BC. None matched the great kings of the past. Over about a century, the New Kingdom slowly came apart: the empire in Asia was lost, prices rose, tombs were robbed, and power shifted to the priests of Amun at Thebes.

Under the later Ramesses (Ramesses IV to XI), Egypt lost its empire in the Levant, royal tombs were robbed and investigated, and the high priests of Amun at Thebes grew powerful. By the end, the high priest ruled the south and a governor named Smendes ruled the north.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The late New Kingdom: a long wind-down after Ramesses III.

items: The empire: by the reign of Ramesses VI, Egyptian rule in Canaan had ended.
Grain: prices at Thebes rose sharply under the later Ramesses.
Security: Libyan groups raided around Thebes, and work at Deir el-Medina was often stopped.
Tomb robbery: under Ramesses IX, officials investigated robberies of royal tombs; the trial records, such as the Abbott and Leopold-Amherst papyri, survive.
Priests: a high priest of Amun had himself shown at the same size as Ramesses IX, a sign of new power.

blocks.html: The empire had paid for much of the New Kingdom's wealth. As it was lost, and as the wider Bronze Age world collapsed, income fell. The temple of Amun at Thebes, endowed with land and wealth for centuries, became an independent power. A weaker king in the distant north could not stop the high priests from taking charge of the south.

Under Ramesses XI, the high priests of Amun (Herihor and Piankh; which came first is debated) ruled Thebes, using some royal titles, while Smendes governed from the Delta. The Report of Wenamun, a story set in these years, tells of an envoy of Amun who sails to Byblos for cedar and is treated with scorn there, a far cry from the days of empire. Whether it is a real report or a literary work is debated.

blocks.title: Sudden or slow?
blocks.q: Was the end of the New Kingdom a single dramatic event?
steps: The empire was lost over decades, under several kings.
Robberies, rising prices and strikes are spread across many reigns.
The high priests gained power step by step until Ramesses XI's death.
blocks.a: No: a slow decline of about a century.

blocks.html: Expecting a sudden fall. The New Kingdom wound down over about a century. A check: date each sign of trouble; they are spread across the 20th Dynasty.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10

blocks.html: At the end of the New Kingdom, c. 1069 BC, Egypt split into a northern kingdom and a southern one run by priests. For nearly four centuries, the Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069–664 BC), power stayed divided, shared among kings, priests and local chiefs.

In the Third Intermediate Period, kings at Tanis in the Delta (the 21st Dynasty), and then Libyan dynasties (the 22nd and 23rd), ruled the north, while the high priests of Amun held Thebes. Later the country broke into many small realms, until the Kushite kings took over.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The centers of a divided Egypt: Tanis and Bubastis in the Delta, Thebes in the south.

blocks.html: The 21st Dynasty kings built their capital at Tanis, reusing statues and blocks brought from older sites such as Pi-Ramesses. In 1939–40 the French archaeologist Pierre Montet found royal tombs inside the temple enclosure at Tanis, including that of Psusennes I with a silver coffin and a gold mask: a treasure that rivals Tutankhamun's.

At Thebes the high priests ran the south and, faced with robbers, moved the mummies of New Kingdom kings from their tombs into hidden caches for safety. One cache, at Deir el-Bahari, was found in the 1870s and cleared in 1881, with Seti I, Ramesses II and many others.

Since the late New Kingdom, families of Libyan origin had settled in Egypt, many as soldiers. Their chiefs became powerful in the Delta, and one, Shoshenq I, took the throne. Libyan rule tended to share power out: the king's sons became high priests and governors of towns, and over time these became hereditary local princes. The result was many centers of power instead of one.

blocks.title: Overlapping dynasties
blocks.q: The 22nd Dynasty is dated c. 945–715 BC and the 25th c. 747–656 BC. Could they have ruled at the same time?
steps: The 25th starts c. 747 BC, before the 22nd ends c. 715 BC.
So for about 30 years both existed.
They ruled different regions: the 22nd in the Delta, the Kushite kings from Napata, spreading north.
blocks.a: Yes: they overlapped, ruling different parts of the land.

blocks.html: Thinking "intermediate" means nothing happened. Temples were built and decorated, fine bronze statues were cast, and trade went on. Power was shared out among many rulers, which makes the period complicated, not empty.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 12, The Third Intermediate Period

blocks.html: In the divided Egypt of the 8th century BC, the strongest power in the Nile valley was not Egyptian. Far to the south, at Napata below the Fourth Cataract, kings of Kush had built a new kingdom that worshipped Amun and saw itself as the true guardian of Egyptian tradition. Then it moved north.

Kings from Kush, such as Piye and Taharqo, conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty (c. 747–656 BC), until the Assyrians drove them out. They saw themselves as rightful pharaohs, restoring temples and old traditions.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Napata and Nuri in Kush, Thebes, and Memphis and Sais in the north.

blocks.html: Around c. 728 BC, a coalition of northern rulers led by Tefnakht of Sais pushed south. Piye sailed north with his army, took Hermopolis and Memphis, and received the submission of the Delta kings. His great Victory Stela, set up in the temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal near Napata, tells the story. It shows a pious king who celebrates Amun's festivals on the way, and who is angrier at a defeated ruler for starving his horses than for fighting him. Then Piye went home to Napata.

items: Shabaqo brought all Egypt under direct Kushite rule. A text he had copied onto stone, the Shabaqo Stone, preserves the Memphite creation account.
Taharqo (c. 690–664 BC) built at Karnak, Jebel Barkal and elsewhere, and was buried in the largest pyramid at Nuri.
Kushite art looked back to the Old and Middle Kingdoms, deliberately reviving older styles.

blocks.html: The kings of Kush had worshipped Amun for centuries, since the New Kingdom built a temple to him at Jebel Barkal. To them, Egypt's divided state was a failure of order, and ruling it was a sacred duty. That is why they presented themselves not as foreign conquerors but as pharaohs restoring maat.

Assyria, the great power of the Near East, now pushed into Egypt. The Assyrian king Esarhaddon took Memphis c. 671 BC; Taharqo retreated south. His successor Tantamani tried to retake Egypt, and in 663 BC the army of Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes. The Kushite kings withdrew to Kush, where their kingdom went on for another thousand years, later centered at Meroë.

blocks.title: Foreign or Egyptian?
blocks.q: Piye and Taharqo came from Kush, worshipped Amun and used the full royal titulary. How did they present themselves?
steps: They took the titles and roles of pharaohs.
They restored Egyptian temples and copied old Egyptian art.
They claimed to restore order in a divided land.
blocks.a: As true heirs of the pharaohs, not as outsiders.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians always ruled Nubia. Here Nubian kings ruled Egypt, from the Delta to the Fourth Cataract, and saw themselves as true heirs of the pharaohs.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 12
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (Chicago, 1906), the stela of Piankhi (Piye)

blocks.html: When the Kushite kings left, the Assyrians backed a family of rulers from Sais in the western Delta. One of them, Psamtek I, became king in 664 BC and, within about eight years, brought the whole country under his rule. From 664 BC on, Egyptian dates are fixed to the year.
Psamtek I, king from 664 BC, reunited Egypt from Sais. The 26th (Saite) Dynasty (664–525 BC) copied Old Kingdom art, built a strong, wealthy state, and welcomed Greek traders and soldiers.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Sais and the Greek trading town of Naukratis in the western Delta.

items: He began as a vassal of Assyria, but as Assyria weakened he acted on his own.
He hired soldiers from Ionia and Caria, in what is now western Turkey.
In 656 BC he had his daughter Nitocris adopted at Thebes as the future God's Wife of Amun, the priestess who stood at the head of Amun's cult there. That brought the south under his rule peacefully.

blocks.html: A divided Egypt needed money and soldiers to unite it. Greek and Carian mercenaries gave Psamtek a loyal army that owed nothing to the local Libyan chiefs, and trade with the Greek world brought wealth. At the same time, reviving the art and titles of the Old Kingdom presented the new dynasty as heir to Egypt's greatest age.

blocks.title: Looking back
blocks.q: A Saite statue looks so much like Old Kingdom work that experts once dated it two thousand years too early. Why?
steps: Saite artists studied and copied Old Kingdom tombs and statues on purpose.
Officials even revived Old Kingdom titles.
So style alone can mislead; inscriptions and details are needed to date the work.
blocks.a: Because Saite art deliberately copied the Old Kingdom.

blocks.html: Skipping the Late Period as a time of decline. The Saite kings ran a strong, wealthy state, with an army, a navy, trade with Greece and a great revival of art and learning.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 13, The Late Period

blocks.html: The Saite kingdom fell to the largest empire the world had yet seen. In 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses II defeated Psamtek III at Pelusium, on Egypt's eastern edge, and took Memphis. Egypt became a province of the Persian Empire.

Cambyses of Persia conquered Egypt in 525 BC; Persian kings ruled it as the 27th Dynasty until 404 BC. They ruled through a governor (a satrap) at Memphis and appeared in Egyptian temples as pharaohs.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The Late Period: the Saite Dynasty, the first Persian rule (27th Dynasty), the last native dynasties, and a second Persian rule before Alexander.

blocks.html: The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about 75 years later, describes Cambyses as cruel and mad: he says he killed the sacred Apis bull and mocked Egyptian gods. Egyptian evidence gives a different picture. An Apis bull that died in Cambyses' reign was buried with full honors, with an inscription naming him. And an Egyptian official, Udjahorresnet, says on his statue that he served Cambyses as an adviser, gave him an Egyptian throne name, and persuaded him to restore the temple of Neith at Sais.

Each source had reasons for its picture. Herodotus heard stories in Egypt decades later, when memories of the conquest were bitter, and he wrote for Greeks who had fought Persia. Udjahorresnet had served the conquerors and wanted to show that he had done good for his gods and his town. Historians weigh both, together with the Apis burial and other documents.

items: Darius I completed a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea, set up stelae along it in Egyptian and in Persian cuneiform, and decorated a temple of Amun at Hibis in Kharga Oasis.
At Elephantine, papyri in Aramaic, the empire's official language, show a garrison of Jewish soldiers serving Persia.
Egyptians rebelled more than once, and in 404 BC they threw the Persians out.

blocks.title: Weighing two sources
blocks.q: Herodotus says Cambyses killed the Apis bull. An Apis epitaph from his reign records a full, honored burial. How should a historian use these?
steps: The epitaph is a document from the time, made in Egypt.
Herodotus wrote about 75 years later, from stories he heard.
The contemporary document counts for more on this point, though Persian rule may still have been harsh in other ways.
blocks.a: Give more weight to the contemporary Egyptian evidence, while keeping both in view.

blocks.html: Repeating Herodotus's stories of Cambyses' cruelty as fact. Egyptian records of his reign paint a milder picture, and scholars weigh the two. A check: when was each source written, and by whom?

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 13

blocks.html: In 404 BC, as Persian power in Egypt broke down, an Egyptian named Amyrtaeus of Sais claimed the throne. For about sixty years, three short native dynasties ruled. They were the last Egyptian-born kings of an independent Egypt until modern times.

Egyptian kings ruled again from 404 BC until Persia returned in 343 BC: the 28th, 29th and 30th Dynasties. Nectanebo II, of the 30th Dynasty, was the last native pharaoh. After him came Persian kings, then Alexander and the Greek Ptolemies.

blocks.html: The 30th Dynasty kings were great builders. Nectanebo I and Nectanebo II added to temples all over Egypt; the oldest standing building at Philae is a gateway hall of Nectanebo I, and he lined the avenue between Karnak and Luxor with sphinxes bearing his name. Their style led straight into the Ptolemaic temples.

Independence had to be defended. The Persians tried several times to win Egypt back, and the native kings paid Greek mercenaries and generals to help hold them off. In 343 BC the Persian king Artaxerxes III finally broke through, and Nectanebo II fled south. Egypt was a Persian province again, now for only eleven years.

blocks.title: The last pharaoh?
blocks.q: Cleopatra VII ruled Egypt until 30 BC. Nectanebo II lost his throne in 343 BC. Who is called the last native pharaoh, and why?
steps: Cleopatra belonged to the Ptolemies, a Macedonian Greek family that came with Alexander.
Nectanebo II was an Egyptian, born into an Egyptian dynasty.
So Nectanebo II was the last native-born king; Cleopatra was the last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty.
blocks.a: Nectanebo II: the last Egyptian-born pharaoh. Cleopatra was the last Ptolemaic ruler.

blocks.html: Later Egyptians told legends about Nectanebo II; one, in the Greek Alexander Romance, made him the secret father of Alexander the Great. That is a legend, but it shows how much Egyptians wanted their last king to live on.
Thinking Cleopatra was the last Egyptian pharaoh. She was Macedonian Greek by family; Nectanebo II was the last native-born king. Cleopatra was the last of the Ptolemies.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 13

blocks.html: In 333 BC Alexander of Macedon defeated the Persian king Darius III at Issus, in what is now southern Turkey. The next year he marched down the coast of the Levant toward Egypt, which had been under Persian rule again since 343 BC.

Alexander the Great took Egypt from Persia in 332 BC: the Persian governor gave it up without a fight. Alexander visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa and founded Alexandria (331 BC), then left to continue his war.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Alexander's Egypt: Memphis, Alexandria on the coast, and the far-off oasis of Siwa in the Western Desert.

blocks.text: Why there was no great battle

blocks.html: The Persian satrap in Egypt, Mazaces, had few troops after Issus and no hope of help. He surrendered the country. Many Egyptians had no love for Persian rule, and Alexander took care to honor Egyptian gods: Greek writers say he sacrificed to the Apis bull at Memphis.

items: Siwa: Alexander crossed the desert to the oasis of Siwa, whose oracle of Amun (the Greeks called him Zeus Ammon) was famous across the Greek world. Ancient writers say the priest greeted him as the son of the god. What was asked and answered was private, and later writers disagree.
Alexandria: on the coast west of the Delta, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, Alexander founded a city that became the capital of Egypt for nearly a thousand years.

A pharaoh: Egyptian temples gave Alexander royal titles and cartouches. Later his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and his son Alexander IV were named in cartouches too, and a granite shrine at Karnak bears Philip's name.

blocks.html: A conqueror who wanted to rule Egypt, not just raid it, needed the support of its temples and people. Being greeted as the son of Amun, and named as pharaoh in Egyptian temples, put Alexander in the place of the king in the Egyptian order. His successors, the Ptolemies, followed the same path.

blocks.title: Counting the years
blocks.q: Persia reconquered Egypt in 343 BC, and Alexander arrived in 332 BC. How long did the second Persian rule last?
steps: Both dates are BC, so subtract the smaller from the larger.
blocks.a: About 11 years.

blocks.html: Alexander left Egypt in 331 BC and died at Babylon in 323 BC. His general Ptolemy took charge of Egypt and brought Alexander's body to be buried there.
Thinking Alexander fought a great battle for Egypt. The Persian governor gave it up without a fight; the great battles were at Issus before, and Gaugamela after.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 14, The Ptolemaic Period

blocks.html: When Alexander died in 323 BC, his generals divided his empire. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, took Egypt, first as governor and from 305 BC as king. His family ruled Egypt for nearly three hundred years, longer than any of the native dynasties of the New Kingdom.

Ptolemy I and his heirs ruled from Alexandria, with its Library, Museum and great lighthouse (the Pharos), as Greek kings to the Greeks and as pharaohs to the Egyptians. They built and rebuilt great Egyptian temples, such as Edfu and Philae.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Alexandria and the great Ptolemaic temples of Upper Egypt.

blocks.cap: How the Ptolemies ruled two peoples.

blocks.html: A small Greek-speaking ruling class governed millions of Egyptians. To keep Egypt peaceful and productive, the Ptolemies needed the temples, which owned land, kept records and spoke for the gods. Building temples, honoring sacred animals and taking part in Egyptian rites won the priests' support. The priests' decrees, like the one on the Rosetta Stone, praised the king in return.

items: The Museum (a shrine of the Muses) was a research institute where scholars lived and worked, paid by the king.
The Library tried to collect every book in Greek; it was the greatest library of the ancient world.
The Pharos lighthouse, finished around 280 BC under Ptolemy II, stood over 100 m high and became one of the Seven Wonders.
Manetho wrote his history of Egypt for the early Ptolemies.

blocks.title: Reading the Rosetta Stone
blocks.q: The Rosetta Stone (196 BC) records a decree of Egyptian priests honoring Ptolemy V, written in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Why three scripts?
steps: Hieroglyphs were the sacred script of temples.
Demotic was the everyday Egyptian script of documents.
Greek was the language of the king and the government.
blocks.a: So that priests, ordinary literate Egyptians and Greek officials could all read it.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: The three texts of the Rosetta Stone and how much of each survives.

blocks.html: Thinking the Ptolemies ignored Egyptian religion. They built and rebuilt great Egyptian temples, like Edfu, Dendera, Kom Ombo and Philae, and appear on their walls making offerings as pharaohs.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 14

blocks.html: The last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty is also the most famous woman of the ancient world. Cleopatra VII came to the throne in 51 BC at about eighteen, sharing it at first with her younger brother. She ruled at a time when Rome had become the master of the Mediterranean, and her kingdom survived only as long as she could deal with Rome's leaders.
Cleopatra VII, allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony, lost to Octavian at the battle of Actium (31 BC). After her death in 30 BC, Egypt became a Roman province.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: The name Cleopatra in hieroglyphs, spelled with sound signs: Champollion used a Cleopatra cartouche from the Philae obelisk (a different, earlier Cleopatra) to help decipher hieroglyphs.

head: Year
Event
rows: Cleopatra becomes queen with her brother Ptolemy XIII
Julius Caesar arrives in Alexandria and takes her side in a war with her brother
her son by Caesar, Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion), is born
she meets Mark Antony at Tarsus and becomes his ally and partner
Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at sea off Actium, in western Greece
Octavian takes Alexandria; Antony and Cleopatra take their own lives; Egypt becomes Roman
blocks.cap: The main events of her reign.

blocks.html: Rome needed Egypt's grain and wealth, and Rome's leaders were at war with each other. A queen of Egypt could survive only by allying with the strongest Roman. Cleopatra chose Caesar, and then Antony, who controlled the eastern half of Rome's world. When Antony lost the struggle with Octavian, she lost her kingdom.

Almost everything written about Cleopatra in antiquity was written by Romans: poets of Octavian's time, who called her a dangerous foreign queen, and historians like Plutarch and Cassius Dio, writing a century or two later. Plutarch says she was the first of her dynasty to learn Egyptian and spoke many languages, and that her charm lay in her conversation more than her looks. Her own coins, temple reliefs and documents give other glimpses: a ruler who appears at Dendera as a pharaoh with her son Caesarion.

blocks.title: Weighing a portrait
blocks.q: A Roman poem written just after Actium calls Cleopatra a mad queen plotting to destroy Rome. How reliable is it as a picture of her?
steps: It was written by a supporter of Octavian, her enemy, right after his victory.
Its purpose was to celebrate Octavian and make the war look like a defense against a foreign threat.
So it tells us more about Roman propaganda than about Cleopatra herself.
blocks.a: Not very reliable as a portrait: it is victors' propaganda.

blocks.html: Taking the Roman picture of Cleopatra as fact. Most surviving accounts were written by her enemies or long after. A check: ask who wrote it, when, and for whom.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 14

blocks.html: After Cleopatra's death in 30 BC, Octavian, soon to be the emperor Augustus, made Egypt part of the Roman Empire. But it was not an ordinary province. For more than six centuries, Egypt was ruled by Rome and then by the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire.

Rome ruled Egypt as a special province: governed by a prefect appointed by the emperor, with Roman senators forbidden to enter without permission. Egypt's grain fed the city of Rome. Egyptian temples, gods and writing went on for centuries.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Roman and Byzantine Egypt, 30 BC to AD 641.

blocks.html: Whoever held Egypt held a vast supply of grain and a fortune in taxes. Augustus did not want a rival senator to take Egypt and starve Rome, so he kept it under his personal control, ruled by a prefect of the equestrian class (a rank below the senators). Grain ships sailed every year from Alexandria to Italy.

items: Papyri: the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus and other towns held huge numbers of Greek documents: tax receipts, letters, contracts, school exercises and lost works of literature.
Portraits: mummies from the Faiyum and elsewhere had painted portraits on wood placed over the face, in a Greco-Roman style.
Temples: emperors appear on temple walls as pharaohs, with their names in cartouches; the temple at Dendera was finished under Rome.
Citizens: in AD 212 the emperor Caracalla made nearly all free people of the empire, Egyptians included, Roman citizens.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Roman Egypt: Alexandria, Oxyrhynchus, the Faiyum, the Red Sea port of Berenike, and the temples of Dendera and Philae.

blocks.html: Hieroglyphs were carved, though by fewer and fewer priests. The last known hieroglyphic inscription, at Philae, dates from AD 394. Demotic was written until the 5th century AD. Over the same centuries, Christianity spread, and Egyptians began writing their language in a new alphabet, Coptic.

blocks.title: Counting across BC and AD
blocks.q: How many years passed between Egypt becoming Roman (30 BC) and the last known hieroglyphic inscription (AD 394)?
steps: There is no year 0, so from 30 BC to AD 394 is 30 + 394 − 1 years.
blocks.a: 423 years. Egyptian writing outlived Cleopatra by more than four centuries.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptian culture ended with the Romans. Temples were still built and hieroglyphs carved for centuries; Roman emperors appear on temple walls as pharaohs.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 15, The Roman Period

blocks.html: Christianity reached Egypt early. Church tradition says the evangelist Mark founded the church of Alexandria in the 1st century AD. By the 4th century, Egypt was one of the great centers of the Christian world, and it gave Christianity something new: monks.

Christianity spread through Egypt in the Roman period. Antony and Pachomius founded monastic life: Antony as a hermit in the desert, Pachomius with the first communities of monks living by a rule. Coptic, Egyptian written in an alphabet based on Greek, became the Christian Egyptians' written language.

items: Antony (about AD 251–356) gave away his property and went into the desert to live alone in prayer. His life, written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, made him famous across the Christian world.
Pachomius (about AD 292–348) gathered monks into communities at Tabennisi in Upper Egypt, with a shared rule of prayer, work and meals. This kind of monastery spread across the Christian world.
Alexandria had a famous school of Christian learning, with teachers like Clement and Origen.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: Coptic: the Egyptian language written in Greek letters plus a few letters taken from Demotic.

blocks.html: Writing Egyptian in Greek letters, with a few extra signs for sounds Greek lacked, made it far easier to learn than hieroglyphs or Demotic, and it showed vowels. Christians needed scriptures and prayers that ordinary Egyptians could read and hear in their own language, and Coptic gave them that.

Old temples closed over a long time, not in a single year. Under the emperor Theodosius I, laws of the AD 390s banned pagan sacrifice, and the great temple of Serapis at Alexandria was destroyed in AD 391. Yet at Philae, on Egypt's southern border, priests still carved the last known hieroglyphic inscription in AD 394, and worship of Isis there went on until the emperor Justinian closed the temple in the AD 530s.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Philae, one of the last temples to close, and Nag Hammadi, where a jar of Coptic books was found in 1945.

blocks.title: One year or many?
blocks.q: A book says "Egyptian religion ended in AD 391." What does the evidence from Philae suggest?
steps: In AD 391 the Serapeum at Alexandria was destroyed.
At Philae, a hieroglyphic inscription was carved in AD 394, and the temple worked until the AD 530s.
So the old religion faded over more than a century, at different times in different places.
blocks.a: That it ended gradually, not in one year.

blocks.html: In AD 451 the Council of Chalcedon split the churches over how to describe Christ's nature. Most Egyptian Christians rejected its decision, and their church, today's Coptic Orthodox Church, went its own way.
Dating the end of Egyptian religion to one year. Old temples closed over a long time; Philae was among the last, in the AD 530s.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 15

blocks.html: In the early 7th century AD, the Byzantine Empire, ruling Christian Egypt from Constantinople, was exhausted by a long war with Persia; the Persians even held Egypt for about ten years, from AD 619. Soon after the Byzantines returned, a new power arose in Arabia.

Arab armies under Amr ibn al-As entered Egypt in AD 639, took the fortress of Babylon (in today's Old Cairo) in AD 641, and then won Alexandria by treaty, ending Byzantine rule. Egypt became part of the Islamic caliphate.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The fortress of Babylon, at the head of the Delta, and Alexandria on the coast.

items: AD 639: Amr crossed from Sinai with a small army; early in AD 640 he took Pelusium.
AD 640: he defeated a Byzantine army near Heliopolis.
AD 641: after a siege, the fortress of Babylon surrendered; later that year the Byzantine authorities agreed to give up Alexandria.
AD 642: the Byzantine garrison sailed away from Alexandria.

blocks.html: Babylon guarded the point where the Nile valley opens into the Delta, the same strategic spot that made Memphis the capital in ancient times. Taking it cut Upper Egypt off from the Byzantine forces in the Delta. Amr founded a new capital beside it, Fustat, which grew into part of Cairo.

Christians and Jews kept their religion, paying a special tax. Greek and Coptic remained in use in government for decades; Arabic became the language of administration early in the 8th century. Over the following centuries more and more Egyptians became Muslim and spoke Arabic, but this took a very long time. Coptic was spoken in some villages for many centuries, and it is still the language of worship of the Coptic Orthodox Church today.

blocks.title: Where to end the course?
blocks.q: Why do many histories of ancient Egypt end in AD 641?
steps: For about a thousand years, since Alexander, Egypt had been ruled from the Greek and Roman world.
In AD 641 it passed into the Islamic world, with a new capital, new rulers and, in time, a new language and majority religion.
Historians treat this as the turning point from ancient to medieval Egypt, even though change came slowly.
blocks.a: Because the conquest ended Byzantine rule and began Egypt's Islamic history, a major turning point.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians changed language and religion at once. Coptic and Christianity remained widespread for centuries; the shift to Arabic and Islam was gradual. A check: Coptic Christians are still a large community in Egypt today.

Every period of Egyptian history is organized around kings. To understand why, you need to know what Egyptians thought a king was. The answer was not "a man with power", or not only that. The king held an office that linked the world of the gods to the world of people.

The king was Horus on earth and the son of Ra, standing between the gods and the people. He offered to the gods, kept maat (right order), and defeated chaos. His five names, the royal titulary, expressed this role.
