blocks.html: The Egyptians believed the world had been created out of chaos, and chaos always threatened to return. Someone had to keep the gods content and order in place. In theory only the king could make offerings in every temple; priests acted in his name. So the office of king was the hinge of the whole order, and his names announced which gods stood behind him.

The office was divine, but the person was human. Kings could be plotted against: Amenemhat I was murdered, and conspiracies in the palace were tried in court under Pepi I and Ramesses III. Literary tales could even poke fun at a king. A king who failed in war or let order slip could be judged harshly by later generations. The word pharaoh comes from pr-ꜥꜣ, "Great House", the palace; from the New Kingdom on it was used for the king himself.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: pr-ꜥꜣ, "the Great House": the palace, and later the king.

blocks.title: Which name?
blocks.q: A cartouche follows the words zꜣ-rꜥ, "son of Ra". Which of the king's five names is it?
steps: Only two of the five names are written in cartouches: the throne name and the birth name.
The throne name follows nsw-bjt; the birth name follows zꜣ-rꜥ.
So this cartouche holds the birth name.
blocks.a: The birth name (the nomen), such as Ramesses.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians saw the living king as all-powerful and beyond criticism. The office was divine; the king could still be criticized, plotted against, or fail. Keep the office and the person apart.
Reading the royal names in hieroglyphs is taught in Middle Egyptian I.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), Introduction
Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (Oxford, 1927), Excursus A, the royal titulary

blocks.html: The king stood at the top, but he did not run the country alone. Egypt was governed by trained officials who kept records of almost everything: land, people, cattle, grain, tools and taxes.

A vizier ran the government for the king, with scribes and officials who surveyed fields, counted harvests and herds, collected taxes and kept the records. In the provinces, governors and town mayors did the same work locally.

The vizier (in Egyptian ṯꜣtj) was the king's chief minister: he heard legal cases, received reports, checked the treasury and granaries, and sent orders across the land. From the New Kingdom there were usually two viziers, one for the north and one for the south. A text called the Duties of the Vizier, carved in the tomb of Rekhmire, vizier under Thutmose III, describes his daily work: hearing petitions, receiving the report of the treasury, keeping watch over the land.

head: Department
What it did
rows: stored precious metals, cloth and goods; paid for state works
collected grain taxes and paid out rations
organized work crews for quarries, building and expeditions
governors and mayors who collected taxes and kept order locally
huge estates with their own officials, often working with the state
blocks.cap: Parts of the government (simplified).

blocks.html: A state that taxed grain had to know how much grain there was. That meant measuring fields after each flood, counting herds, recording the harvest and writing it all down. Writing and counting were the tools of power, and scribes who mastered them were the people who made the state work.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: An Egyptian number: one lotus (1,000), three coils (300), five hobbles (50) and two strokes (2). Accounts of grain and cattle were full of numbers like this.

blocks.html: Boys from official families, and some from humbler ones, learned to read and write in schools attached to temples and offices, copying model letters and classic texts. A popular school text, the Teaching of Khety, praises the scribe's life and mocks every other job. Only a small minority of Egyptians could read and write, which is one reason scribes held such power.

blocks.title: Reading a record
blocks.q: A scribe writes a cattle count as one lotus, three coils, five hobbles and two strokes. How many cattle?
steps: A lotus is 1,000; a coil is 100; a hobble is 10; a stroke is 1.
blocks.a: 1,352 cattle.

blocks.html: Imagining the king did everything. Most governing was done by trained officials, from the vizier down to village scribes. Kings set policy and took the credit; officials did the work.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9
James Henry Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (Chicago, 1906), the duties of the vizier (tomb of Rekhmire)

blocks.html: The officials counted grain and goods. But how did ordinary people buy and sell? For most of its history, Egypt had a rich economy without any coins at all.

Until the Late Period, Egyptians did not use coins. They traded goods directly, valuing them in units of copper (the deben, about 91 g in the New Kingdom) or of grain (the khar, a sack of about 77 liters). Wages were paid in rations of bread, beer and grain.

Money does three jobs: it measures value, it is a way to pay, and it stores wealth. In Egypt the deben did the first job, measuring value, without having to change hands. A buyer could pay with any goods worth the same number of deben. Grain, which everyone needed, was the most common way to pay and to store wealth.

blocks.title: A purchase in deben
blocks.q: In the style of the Deir el-Medina records: a man buys a bed valued at 20 deben. He pays with a goat worth 8 deben, two pairs of sandals worth 1 deben each, and some grain. How many deben' worth of grain must he add?
steps: Goods paid so far: 8 + 1 + 1 = 10 deben.
Still owed: 20 − 10 = 10 deben.
He adds grain worth 10 deben.
blocks.a: 10 deben of grain. No copper changes hands at all.

blocks.html: State workers were paid in kind. The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina received monthly rations of grain, about 4 khar of emmer wheat and 1½ khar of barley for a workman, more for the foremen, plus fish, vegetables, oil and firewood. Emmer was made into bread and barley into beer. When rations were late, people went hungry, which is why the workmen went on strike under Ramesses III.

head: Unit
What it measures
Size
rows: value, in weight of copper (or silver)
blocks.cap: Units of value.

blocks.html: Coins were invented in Lydia and the Greek world in the 7th century BC. Greek coins reached Egypt in the Late Period, mostly to be weighed as silver. Egypt's own first coins came under the 30th Dynasty: small gold coins bearing the hieroglyphs nfr nbw, "good gold", probably to pay Greek soldiers. Only under the Ptolemies did coins come into everyday use.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nfr, "good", and nbw, "gold": together, the words on Egypt's first gold coins.

blocks.html: Assuming money meant coins. Egyptians priced things in deben without needing coins, and paid with goods of equal value. A check: a price in deben tells you the value, not what was handed over.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10

blocks.html: Kings and officials left the most monuments, but they were a tiny part of the population. Most Egyptians were farmers who left no written words of their own. To see Egyptian society whole, we have to look at all its layers.

Most Egyptians were farmers. Above them were craftsmen, scribes, priests and officials, with the king at the top. There were servants and some slaves, especially war captives in the New Kingdom. Egypt was a ranked society, but slavery did not build the pyramids.

head: Group
Life and work
rows: the great majority: they worked land owned by the state, temples or estates, paid part of the harvest as tax, and could be called up for labor
carpenters, potters, stone carvers, painters, metalworkers, often working for temples and the state
the small literate class who ran the government, temples and estates
many served part-time in shifts, returning to ordinary life between turns
from the New Kingdom a professional army, rewarded with land
household servants; captives taken in war and given to temples, estates and officials
blocks.cap: The people of Egypt (simplified).

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: rmṯ, "people", with the determinatives of a man and a woman and the plural strokes.

blocks.html: The whole economy rested on farming the land along the Nile. A small group with land, education and office could live off the surplus of many farmers. That made the society steeply ranked. But Egyptians did not see the ranks as completely closed: some texts praise men who rose by ability, and a farmer's son could sometimes become a scribe.

Egypt did have slaves, and their number grew in the New Kingdom, when campaigns brought back captives who were given to temples and officials. Some people were sold into servitude, and slaves could be bought and sold, though they could also own property and be freed. The great building projects of the Old Kingdom, however, were done by organized Egyptian crews, paid in rations and partly called up for a season.

blocks.title: Who built the pyramids?
blocks.q: A film shows the Great Pyramid built by slaves under the whip. What does the evidence from Giza say?
steps: The workers' town had bakeries and breweries, and the workers' tombs had grave goods and inscriptions.
Skeletons show healed injuries, a sign of care.
So the workforce was organized and fed Egyptian labor, not a mass of slaves.
blocks.a: Egyptian crews, organized by the state.

blocks.html: Picturing a land of slaves, or a land of equals. Egypt was a ranked society; slavery existed, especially for war captives in the New Kingdom, but it did not build the pyramids.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9 and 10

blocks.html: Most ordinary Egyptians left no words. One village is the great exception. In a narrow valley on the west bank at Thebes lived the craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings, and they wrote, and wrote, and wrote.

The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs lived at Deir el-Medina (ancient name: Set-maat, "the Place of Truth"). Thousands of their notes on ostraca, flakes of limestone and pieces of pottery, survive, along with papyri, giving the names, work, quarrels, debts and jokes of ordinary workers.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Deir el-Medina, a short walk over the hill from the Valley of the Kings.

items: Founded early in the 18th Dynasty and lived in until the end of the 20th, about 450 years.
About seventy houses inside a wall, each with a few rooms in a row, plus more houses outside.
The crew was split into a "right side" and a "left side", each with a foreman, plus a scribe who kept the records.
They worked in shifts, sleeping near the tomb during their working days, then walked home over the hill for days off.
They built their own fine tombs, with small pyramids, on the hillside above the village.

blocks.html: These men were skilled, literate or partly literate, and paid by the state, and they lived in a dry place where limestone flakes for writing lay everywhere. Notes that elsewhere would have been written on papyrus and lost were scratched on stone and kept. The excavations of Bernard Bruyère and others in the 1900s recovered them by the thousand.

Example

family letters, school copies of classic texts, love songs, sketches
blocks.cap: The village's writings.

blocks.title: Reading a register
blocks.q: A work register lists a man as absent because he was "brewing beer". What does that tell a historian?
steps: The scribe recorded absences and their reasons, so work was carefully tracked.
Brewing beer was a normal reason to miss a day, accepted by the foreman.
So we learn both how the state managed labor and what ordinary life included.
blocks.a: That work was closely recorded, and that home life and festivals were part of the workers' rights.

blocks.html: The village also produced the records of the first known strike, and the will of a woman named Naunakhte, which you will meet in Women in Ancient Egypt. Explore the site on the map of Ancient Egypt.
Thinking we know only about kings. Deir el-Medina gives the names, quarrels, debts and jokes of ordinary workers. Remember, though, that these were skilled, well-paid craftsmen, not typical farmers.

blocks.html: We have met powerful women already: Hatshepsut, who ruled as king, and Queen Ahhotep, praised for rallying the army in the Theban war. But what about ordinary women? Here Egypt stands out among ancient societies.

Egyptian women could own and sell property, make contracts, go to court, inherit and leave wills, and keep their own share of property in marriage. Few held office: men held most positions in government, though women served as priestesses and a few as kings.

Around the reign of Ramesses V, a woman of Deir el-Medina named Naunakhte made a will before the village court. She left her own property to the children who had cared for her in old age, and disinherited four who had not. Her late husband's property was another matter: by law it would be shared among all his heirs. The court accepted her decision. This document shows a woman controlling her own wealth and using the law to do it.

Evidence
rows: contracts and sales made by women in their own names
the will of Naunakhte, and many other documents
women appear as parties and witnesses in lawsuits
a private arrangement; either side could end it, and the wife kept a share of the joint property
weaving, baking, brewing, music, mourning, midwifery; priestesses and chantresses in temples

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nbt, "lady, mistress". A married woman was often called nbt pr, "mistress of the house".

blocks.html: Egyptian law treated a woman as a legal person in her own right, able to hold property and act for herself. In many ancient societies, a woman needed a male guardian to do these things. In Egypt she did not. That did not make men and women equal in power: offices, schooling and most public roles belonged to men.

blocks.title: Equal or not?
blocks.q: Women could own land and go to court, yet almost all viziers, governors and scribes were men. How should we describe women's position?
steps: In law, women had real rights over property, contracts and inheritance.
In public life, men held nearly all offices.
So women had more legal rights than in many ancient societies, but not equal power.
blocks.a: Strong legal rights, limited public power.

blocks.html: Assuming ancient women had no rights. Egyptian women had more legal rights than in many ancient societies, though men held most offices. Avoid the opposite mistake too: Egypt was not a land of equality between men and women.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 10

blocks.html: The New Kingdom empire was won by an army very different from the forces of the Old Kingdom. Over two thousand years, Egypt's military changed from part-time levies into a professional standing army with chariots and foreign troops.

Egypt's army grew from local levies raised for campaigns and expeditions into the standing army of the New Kingdom, with chariots, infantry divisions and foreign troops. Horses and chariots came into Egypt around the Second Intermediate Period.

head: Period
The army
rows: levies of men called up by officials for a campaign or a quarry expedition, as Weni describes
more permanent troops; garrisons in the Nubian forts; Nubian scouts called the Medjay
a professional army: chariotry, infantry divisions named after gods, archers with the composite bow, foreign units
Greek and Carian mercenaries alongside Egyptian soldiers

blocks.html: Fighting the Hyksos and then the great powers of Asia demanded something new. A chariot, light and fast, carried a driver and an archer with a powerful composite bow, and could strike, wheel and strike again. Chariots and horses were expensive and needed skilled crews and constant training, which only a full-time, state-paid army could provide.

items: At Kadesh Ramesses II's army marched in four divisions named for Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth.
Charioteers were an elite; the king himself was shown charging in his chariot.
Foreign soldiers served too: Nubian archers, Medjay, and Sherden warriors (from among the Sea Peoples).
Veterans received land, so the army became a class with a stake in the state.

blocks.title: When did chariots arrive?
blocks.q: A drawing shows Khufu's army riding chariots. What is wrong with it?
steps: Khufu reigned c. 2589–2566 BC, in the Old Kingdom.
Horses and chariots came into Egypt around the Second Intermediate Period, c. 1650–1550 BC.
That is about a thousand years after Khufu.
blocks.a: Khufu had no chariots; they arrived about a thousand years later.

blocks.html: Thinking chariots were always Egyptian. Horses and chariots came into Egypt around the Second Intermediate Period, probably from western Asia, and transformed warfare in the New Kingdom.

sources.name: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000), ch. 9

blocks.html: South of the First Cataract lay Nubia, along the Nile in what is now southern Egypt and Sudan. You have met it several times: Harkhuf's journeys, the Middle Kingdom forts, the kingdom of Kerma and the Kushite pharaohs. Now we look at the whole relationship, and at Nubia's own history.
For three thousand years Egypt traded with, fought and ruled parts of Nubia, and Nubian kings once ruled Egypt. Nubian kingdoms, Kerma, Napata and Meroë, had their own long history.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Nubia from the First Cataract to Meroë.

blocks.html: The river tied the two lands together, and the cataracts both slowed and channeled traffic. Nubia had gold, ivory, ebony, incense and fine soldiers, and it stood between Egypt and the lands farther south. Whichever side was stronger at a given time, the other was always there as trading partner, rival and neighbor.

After the Assyrians drove them out of Egypt, the Kushite kings ruled on from Napata and later from Meroë, far to the south. Meroë had iron working, temples to both Egyptian and Nubian gods (such as the lion god Apedemak), steep pyramids for its rulers, and its own script, Meroitic. The script can be read aloud, but the Meroitic language is still only partly understood. The kingdom lasted until about the 4th century AD.

blocks.title: Whose eyes?
blocks.q: Egyptian royal inscriptions often call Kush "wretched". What does that word tell us?
steps: It is a stock phrase of Egyptian royal ideology, applied to foreign enemies.
Archaeology shows Kerma and Meroë as rich, organized kingdoms.
So the word tells us about Egyptian propaganda, not about Kush.
blocks.a: It reflects the Egyptian point of view; it is not a fair description.

blocks.html: Seeing Nubia only through Egyptian eyes. Nubian kingdoms (Kerma, Napata, Meroë) had their own long history, culture and achievements. See all the sites on the map of Ancient Egypt.

blocks.html: Deserts protected Egypt on east and west, but they never cut it off. Across Sinai and along the coast ran roads to the Levant (today's Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria), and ships sailed up the coast to its ports. Beyond lay the great kingdoms of the Near East.
Egypt traded with Byblos for cedar from the Old Kingdom on, ruled parts of Canaan in the New Kingdom, and dealt with the great powers in turn: Mitanni, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon and Persia.

blocks.html: Egypt had grain and gold but almost no good timber, little silver, and no tin for bronze. The Levant and lands beyond had them. Trade made these goods flow; diplomacy kept the trade safe; and when a great power threatened the routes, war followed. The Amarna letters show how busy this world was.

items: Egyptian objects of Old Kingdom kings were dedicated in the temple of Byblos.
In Sinai, at Serabit el-Khadim, workers in the Egyptian turquoise mines left some of the earliest known alphabetic inscriptions.
Gods traveled too: Egyptians took up Levantine gods like Baal and Astarte in the New Kingdom.
Diplomats wrote in Akkadian cuneiform and addressed each other as "brother".

blocks.title: Why Byblos?
blocks.q: Why did Egypt keep trading with Byblos for more than two thousand years?
steps: Egypt had few tall trees; its own wood was poor for big ships and temple doors.
The mountains behind Byblos had cedar forests.
Byblos was a port, so the timber could be shipped by sea to Egypt.
blocks.a: For cedar, which Egypt lacked, shipped from a convenient port.

blocks.html: Treating Egypt as cut off by deserts. It was part of a busy world of trade and diplomacy, from Byblos to Babylon. A check: list the materials an Egyptian temple needed and where each came from.

blocks.html: Egypt appears often in the Hebrew Bible: Joseph rises to power there, the Israelites leave it in the Exodus, and later a pharaoh called Shishak attacks Jerusalem. How do these stories relate to the Egyptian evidence you have learned? Historians and biblical scholars have debated this for two centuries. This lesson lays out the main positions without choosing among them.

Historians debate how the stories of Joseph and the Exodus relate to Egyptian evidence; no Egyptian source mentions either. Many scholars identify Shishak with Shoshenq I of the 22nd Dynasty, though some doubt it. The earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible is on the stela of Merneptah (c. 1208 BC).

blocks.text: What Egyptian sources do and do not say

items: Merneptah Stela (c. 1208 BC): a victory hymn that lists Israel among peoples in Canaan, written with the sign for a people rather than a land.
Shoshenq I (c. 945–924 BC): a relief at Karnak lists towns his army took in Canaan, and a fragment of a stela with his name was found at Megiddo.
No Egyptian text names Joseph, Moses or the Exodus.

blocks.html: These questions are hard because the kinds of evidence differ. The biblical texts were written down long after the events they describe, for religious purposes; Egyptian royal texts rarely mention small groups or defeats; and archaeology rarely names individuals. Scholars weigh the same evidence differently, and new finds keep the discussion going.

blocks.title: Stating a debate fairly
blocks.q: A student writes, "Archaeology proves the Exodus happened under Ramesses II." How could the sentence be made accurate?
steps: No Egyptian source mentions the Exodus, so "proves" claims too much.
Some scholars link the story to the time of Ramesses II; others propose other dates or doubt a historical event.
An accurate version names the positions and the evidence each relies on.
blocks.a: For example: "Some scholars link the Exodus to the time of Ramesses II; others propose other dates, and many doubt the story can be dated at all."

blocks.html: Expecting a simple yes or no. Scholars weigh the evidence differently, and the questions remain open. When you write about them, give the main positions and the evidence, and keep your own beliefs out of the summary.
